title: Mass generation in graphs
summary: We demonstrate a mechanism for the production of massive excitations in graphs. We treat the number of neighbors at each vertex in the graph (degree) as a scalar field. Then we introduce a mechanism inspired by the Higgs mechanism in quantum field theory(QFT), that couples the degree field to a vector-like field, introduced via the graph edges, represented mathematically by the incident matrices of the graph. The coupling between the two fields produces a massless ground state and massive excitations, separated by a mass gap. The excitations can be treated as emergent massive particles, propagating inside the graph. We study how the size of the graph and its density, represented by the ratio of edges over vertices, affects the mass gap and the localization properties of the massive excitations. We show that the most massive excitations, corresponding to the heaviest emergent particles, localize on regions of the graph with high density, consisting of vertices with a large degree. On the other hand, the least massive excitations, corresponding to the lightest emergent particles localize on a few vertices but with a smaller degree. Excitations with intermediate masses are less localized, spreading on more vertices instead. Our study shows that emergence of matter-like structures with various mass properties, is possible in discrete physical models, relying only on a few fundamental properties like the connectivity of the models.

AI.tldr: Graph-based mechanism inspired by Higgs field produces massive excitations as emergent particles with mass gap dependent on graph size and density.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate how matter-like structures with various mass properties can emerge from discrete physical models based solely on connectivity properties, drawing inspiration from quantum field theory's Higgs mechanism.
AI.method: Treat vertex degree as scalar field, introduce vector-like field via graph edges (incident matrices), couple them using Higgs-inspired mechanism to produce massless ground state and massive excitations separated by mass gap.
AI.result: Massive excitations localize based on graph density: heaviest particles localize on high-degree vertices in dense regions, lightest particles localize on few low-degree vertices, intermediate-mass particles spread across more vertices. Mass gap depends on graph size and edge-to-vertex ratio.
AI.conclusion: Matter-like structures with diverse mass properties can emerge from discrete models using only fundamental connectivity properties, providing a framework for studying emergent particle behavior in graph-based systems.

title: Geometry of Free Fermion Commutants
summary: Understanding the structure of operators that commute with $k$ identical replicas of unitary ensembles, also known as their $k$-commutants, is an important problem in quantum many-body physics with deep implications for the late-time behavior of physical quantities such as correlation functions and entanglement entropies under unitary evolution. In this work, we study the $k$-commutants of free-fermion unitary systems, which are heuristically known to contain $SO(k)$ and $SU(k)$ groups without and with particle number conservation respectively, with formal derivations of projectors onto these commutants appearing only very recently. We establish a complementary perspective by highlighting a larger $O(2k)$ replica symmetry (or $SU(2k)$ respectively) that the $k$-commutant transforms irreducibly under, which leads to a simple geometric understanding of the commutant in terms of coherent states parametrized by a Grassmannian manifold. We derive this structure by mapping the $k$-commutant to the ground state of effective ferromagnetic Heisenberg models, analogous to the ones that appear in the noisy circuit literature, which we solve exactly using standard representation theory methods. Further, we show that the Grassmannian manifold of the $k$-commutant is exactly the manifold of fermionic Gaussian states on $2k$ sites, which reveals a duality between real space and replica space in free-fermion systems. This geometric understanding also provides a compact projection formula onto the $k$-commutant, based on the resolution of identity for coherent states, which can prove advantageous in analytical calculations of averaged non-linear functionals of Gaussian states, as we demonstrate using some examples for the entanglement entropies. In all, this work provides a geometric perspective on the $k$-commutant of free-fermions that naturally connects to problems in quantum many-body physics.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a geometric perspective on the k-commutants of free-fermion unitary systems, revealing an O(2k)/SU(2k) replica symmetry and connecting them to Grassmannian manifolds and effective Heisenberg models.
AI.motivation: Understanding k-commutants (operators commuting with k replicas of unitary ensembles) is crucial for studying late-time behavior of quantum many-body systems, but formal derivations for free-fermion systems have only recently appeared.
AI.method: Establishes a larger O(2k)/SU(2k) replica symmetry, maps k-commutants to ground states of effective ferromagnetic Heisenberg models, solves them using representation theory, and connects to Grassmannian manifolds of fermionic Gaussian states.
AI.result: Reveals that k-commutants transform irreducibly under O(2k)/SU(2k) symmetry, are parametrized by Grassmannian manifolds, and provide a compact projection formula based on coherent state resolution of identity.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a geometric perspective connecting k-commutants of free-fermions to quantum many-body physics problems, offering advantages for analytical calculations of averaged non-linear functionals like entanglement entropies.

title: Real-time Dynamics in 3D for up to 1000 Qubits with Neural Quantum States: Quenches and the Quantum Kibble--Zurek Mechanism
summary: Exponential complexity of many-body wave functions limits accurate numerical simulations of real-time dynamics, especially beyond 1D, where rapid entanglement growth poses severe challenges. Neural Quantum States (NQS) have emerged as a powerful approach for real-time dynamics in 2D, but their scalability and accuracy in 3D have remained an open challenge. Here, we establish NQS as a scalable framework for 3D quantum dynamics by introducing a residual-based convolutional architecture tailored to cubic spin lattices. Focusing on the 3D transverse-field Ising model, we demonstrate that NQS reliably capture distinct quench regimes, including collapse-and-revival dynamics and, most challengingly, the dynamics following a sudden quench to the quantum critical point. We perform finite-rate quenches to the critical point on lattices containing up to $1000$ qubits, an unprecedented system size for numerical simulations of real-time dynamics beyond 1D. This enables the first large-scale numerical demonstration of the 3D quantum Kibble--Zurek mechanism. The QKZM in 3D is particularly intriguing because it lies at the upper critical dimension of the Ising universality class, where the standard power laws are modified by logarithmic factors together with prominent sub-leading logarithmic corrections. By deriving these corrections from renormalization-group flow equations up to two-loop order, we obtain a robust data collapse across all simulated system sizes for the correlation function, the excess energy, and the quantum Fisher information, the latter revealing universal multipartite-entanglement dynamics. In all cases, we find compelling agreement with the expected scaling dimensions. Our findings establish NQS as a scalable and reliable tool for exploring nonequilibrium phenomena in 3D quantum matter and for providing numerical benchmarks for 3D quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Neural Quantum States (NQS) with residual-based convolutional architecture enable scalable 3D quantum dynamics simulations of up to 1000 qubits, demonstrating the 3D quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism with logarithmic corrections.
AI.motivation: Exponential complexity limits real-time quantum dynamics simulations beyond 1D, especially in 3D where entanglement growth is rapid. Neural Quantum States have shown promise in 2D but scalability and accuracy in 3D remained an open challenge.
AI.method: Introduce a residual-based convolutional architecture tailored to cubic spin lattices for Neural Quantum States. Apply this to the 3D transverse-field Ising model, performing finite-rate quenches to the critical point on lattices up to 1000 qubits. Derive logarithmic corrections from renormalization-group flow equations up to two-loop order.
AI.result: NQS reliably capture distinct quench regimes including collapse-and-revival dynamics and critical point dynamics. Enable first large-scale demonstration of 3D quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism. Obtain robust data collapse across all system sizes for correlation function, excess energy, and quantum Fisher information, showing agreement with expected scaling dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Neural Quantum States establish as a scalable and reliable tool for exploring nonequilibrium phenomena in 3D quantum matter and providing numerical benchmarks for 3D quantum simulators.

title: Efficient simulation of noisy IQP circuits with amplitude-damping noise
summary: Efficient classical simulation of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) circuits has been a topic of intense study over the past few years. The majority of results on efficient simulation assume that the circuits undergo some variant of unital noise or involve sufficient randomness. However, there are limited results for circuits undergoing non-unital noise in the absence of randomness. In this work, we present a polynomial-time classical algorithm to sample from the output distributions of amplitude-damped instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) circuits. Our algorithm works for circuits generated by arbitrary $l$-local diagonal gates with depth $d = Ω(\log(n))$, undergoing constant amplitude-damping noise.

AI.tldr: Polynomial-time classical algorithm for sampling from amplitude-damped IQP circuits with l-local diagonal gates and depth Ω(log(n)), addressing non-unital noise simulation.
AI.motivation: Most efficient classical simulation results for noisy quantum circuits assume unital noise or randomness; limited results exist for non-unital noise without randomness, creating a gap in simulation capabilities for amplitude-damped NISQ circuits.
AI.method: Developed polynomial-time classical algorithm that samples from output distributions of amplitude-damped IQP circuits generated by arbitrary l-local diagonal gates with depth d = Ω(log(n)), undergoing constant amplitude-damping noise.
AI.result: Algorithm provides efficient classical simulation of amplitude-damped IQP circuits, demonstrating that certain non-unital noise models can be simulated efficiently without requiring randomness assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Amplitude-damped IQP circuits with sufficient depth can be classically simulated efficiently, expanding the known boundaries of classical simulability for noisy quantum circuits beyond unital noise models.

title: Mixed eigenstates in spin-boson systems with one-photon and two-photon interactions
summary: Spin-boson systems have attracted increasing attention as accessible experimental platforms and for their potential applications in designing quantum technologies. One characteristic of these systems is the transition from regular to completely chaotic behavior when certain control parameters are varied. However, the characterization of their mixed phase space has not been thoroughly explored. In this work, we investigate the properties of mixed eigenstates in spin-boson systems, comparing one-photon interactions with two-photon interactions. We propose a generalized definition of the phase-space overlap index to identify genuine mixed eigenstates. Our study highlights the fundamental differences that arise when two-photon processes are considered compared to one-photon processes and provides complementary evidence supporting the validity of the principle of uniform semiclassical condensation (PUSC) of quasiprobability functions in spin-boson systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of mixed eigenstates in spin-boson systems comparing one-photon vs two-photon interactions, proposing generalized phase-space overlap index to identify genuine mixed states and supporting PUSC principle.
AI.motivation: Spin-boson systems show transitions from regular to chaotic behavior but their mixed phase space characterization hasn't been thoroughly explored. Need to understand differences between one-photon and two-photon interactions in these systems.
AI.method: Investigate properties of mixed eigenstates in spin-boson systems, compare one-photon with two-photon interactions, propose generalized definition of phase-space overlap index to identify genuine mixed eigenstates.
AI.result: Study reveals fundamental differences between one-photon and two-photon processes in spin-boson systems, provides complementary evidence supporting validity of principle of uniform semiclassical condensation (PUSC) of quasiprobability functions.
AI.conclusion: The research advances understanding of mixed phase space in spin-boson systems, demonstrates importance of interaction type (one-photon vs two-photon), and validates PUSC principle for these quantum systems.

title: Information Propagation in Rydberg Arrays via Analog OTOC Calculations
summary: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are the main tool for probing quantum chaos and scrambling, and have become crucial probes in many areas of quantum computing. However, the measurement of OTOCs is difficult to implement on analog quantum computers due to the requirement of backward time evolution. In this paper, we develop and implement a randomized measurement protocol to compute OTOCs on Aquila by QuEra Computing. Unlike traditional methods that require backward time evolution, our approach utilizes a sequence of global randomized quenches that approximates the unitary 2-design properties necessary for extracting infinite-temperature OTOCs from statistical correlations. We demonstrate the protocol's success by explicitly observing the lightcone of information propagation in 1D Rydberg chains, and compare hardware results to both state-vector simulations and matrix product state (MPS) tensor network calculations. This work establishes the first demonstration of fully analog randomized OTOC measurements in neutral-atom simulators, providing a scalable pathway to probe quantum chaos in complex many-body systems.

AI.tldr: A randomized measurement protocol for OTOCs on neutral-atom quantum computers that avoids backward time evolution by using global randomized quenches to extract statistical correlations.
AI.motivation: OTOCs are crucial for probing quantum chaos and scrambling but are difficult to measure on analog quantum computers due to the requirement of backward time evolution, which is challenging to implement physically.
AI.method: Developed and implemented a randomized measurement protocol using sequences of global randomized quenches that approximate unitary 2-design properties to extract infinite-temperature OTOCs from statistical correlations, demonstrated on QuEra's Aquila neutral-atom quantum computer.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated the protocol by observing the lightcone of information propagation in 1D Rydberg chains, with hardware results compared to state-vector simulations and MPS tensor network calculations, showing agreement.
AI.conclusion: Established the first demonstration of fully analog randomized OTOC measurements in neutral-atom simulators, providing a scalable pathway to probe quantum chaos in complex many-body systems without requiring backward time evolution.

title: Instability-Enhanced Quantum Sensing with Tunable Multibody Interactions
summary: Dynamical instabilities can amplify small perturbations into measurable signals, offering a route to quantum-enhanced sensing. This mechanism was experimentally demonstrated in a collective-spin system with quadratic interactions, described by a twisting-and-turning Hamiltonian, where quantum evolution near an unstable point leads to exponential growth of spin fluctuations, enabling metrological gain beyond the standard quantum limit. Here, we show that a quartic extension of this Hamiltonian substantially increases the amplification. The additional nonlinear term reshapes the phase-space structure, generating new unstable points and accelerating signal amplification. As a result, enhanced sensitivity is achieved within experimentally accessible coherence times. Remarkably, even at fixed instability rate (equal Lyapunov exponent), multibody interactions outperform the quadratic case due to enhanced short-time dynamics. We analyze the classical and quantum behavior of the multibody model and discuss its experimental implementations. Our results identify phase-space curvature as a resource for optimizing the speed and performance of quantum sensors.

AI.tldr: Adding quartic nonlinearity to a twisting-and-turning Hamiltonian enhances signal amplification for quantum sensing beyond quadratic interactions, achieving better sensitivity within coherence times through modified phase-space curvature.
AI.motivation: Dynamical instabilities can amplify small perturbations for quantum-enhanced sensing, but existing quadratic interactions have limitations. The paper aims to show that adding multibody (quartic) interactions can substantially increase amplification and achieve enhanced sensitivity within practical coherence times.
AI.method: The authors extend the twisting-and-turning Hamiltonian with quadratic interactions to include quartic (four-body) nonlinear terms. They analyze both classical and quantum behavior of this multibody model, examining how the additional nonlinearity reshapes phase-space structure, creates new unstable points, and accelerates signal amplification. They compare performance with the quadratic case at equal instability rates (Lyapunov exponents).
AI.result: The quartic extension substantially increases amplification compared to quadratic interactions. Even at fixed instability rates, multibody interactions outperform quadratic cases due to enhanced short-time dynamics. The modified phase-space structure enables enhanced sensitivity within experimentally accessible coherence times.
AI.conclusion: Phase-space curvature serves as a resource for optimizing quantum sensor speed and performance. Multibody interactions offer superior amplification and sensitivity compared to quadratic interactions, making them promising for practical quantum-enhanced sensing applications.

title: Unlocking a fast adiabatic CZ gate and exact residual $ZZ$ cancellation between fixed-frequency transmons using a floating tunable coupler
summary: Tunable couplers in superconducting qubit architectures enable strong qubit-qubit interactions for two-qubit gates while suppressing unwanted coupling during single-qubit operations. However, achieving low error rates for fast two-qubit gates remains challenging, as suppressing leakage and non-adiabatic errors typically requires specialized qubit, coupler, or pulse designs, often at the expense of an idling $ZZ=0$ condition. In this work, we demonstrate that a symmetric floating tunable coupler provides a natural platform for fast, high-fidelity adiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gates. Its favorable energy-level structure eliminates the conventional trade-off between rapid conditional-phase accumulation and adiabatic evolution while preserving exact cancellation of residual $ZZ$ interaction at idling. This architecture exhibits intrinsic robustness to non-adiabatic transitions, even under simple flux modulation waveforms. To push performance at short gate durations, where maintaining adiabaticity becomes more challenging despite the favorable level structure, we introduce pulse-shaping techniques based on the instantaneous adiabatic factor that further suppress non-adiabatic errors. We experimentally realize a 24 ns adiabatic CZ gate with fidelity exceeding 99.9% and stable operation over several hours.

AI.tldr: A symmetric floating tunable coupler enables fast, high-fidelity adiabatic CZ gates by eliminating the trade-off between conditional-phase accumulation and adiabatic evolution while preserving zero residual ZZ interaction at idling.
AI.motivation: Tunable couplers in superconducting qubits enable strong interactions for two-qubit gates but suppressing leakage and non-adiabatic errors typically requires specialized designs that compromise the idling ZZ=0 condition. Achieving low error rates for fast two-qubit gates remains challenging.
AI.method: Uses a symmetric floating tunable coupler architecture with favorable energy-level structure that eliminates the conventional trade-off. Introduces pulse-shaping techniques based on the instantaneous adiabatic factor to suppress non-adiabatic errors at short gate durations. Experimental implementation with flux modulation waveforms.
AI.result: Demonstrated a 24 ns adiabatic CZ gate with fidelity exceeding 99.9% and stable operation over several hours. The architecture shows intrinsic robustness to non-adiabatic transitions even under simple flux modulation.
AI.conclusion: The symmetric floating tunable coupler provides a natural platform for fast, high-fidelity adiabatic CZ gates, overcoming the conventional limitations of tunable couplers while preserving exact cancellation of residual ZZ interaction at idling.

title: Tennis-racket instability of twisted electrons
summary: We demonstrate that a weak nonlinear magnetic entrance edge induces a tennis-racket (Dzhanibekov) instability in the shell-resolved orbital pseudospin dynamics of twisted electrons propagating in a nominally uniform solenoidal field. Starting from a Maxwell-consistent thin-edge extension of the entrance field, we derive an effective fixed-shell Hamiltonian in which linear Schwinger pseudospin precession acquires an anisotropic quadratic correction. In the symmetric aligned limit, an exact linear eigenstate (a Laguerre-Gaussian vortex state) becomes a hyperbolic fixed point of the large-shell dynamics, producing recurrent reversals of the mean pseudospin projection. These reversals appear in real space as repeated conversions of the transverse profile between Laguerre-Gaussian vortex and Hermite-Gaussian multi-lobed states. The unavoidable Lewis-Ermakov breathing of realistic wave packets does not generate a separate mechanism; it naturally modulates the nonlinear strength and sets the growth time scale. Microscope-scale estimates show that the required regime is accessible with standard octupole correctors in a transmission electron microscope.

AI.tldr: Twisted electrons in solenoidal fields exhibit tennis-racket instability due to weak nonlinear magnetic entrance edges, causing recurrent pseudospin reversals and transverse profile conversions between vortex and multi-lobed states.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that weak nonlinear magnetic entrance edges can induce tennis-racket (Dzhanibekov) instability in the orbital pseudospin dynamics of twisted electrons, revealing novel nonlinear effects in electron vortex beam propagation.
AI.method: Developed a Maxwell-consistent thin-edge extension of the entrance field, derived an effective fixed-shell Hamiltonian with anisotropic quadratic corrections to linear Schwinger pseudospin precession, analyzed symmetric aligned limit dynamics, and examined realistic wave packet breathing effects.
AI.result: Exact linear eigenstate (Laguerre-Gaussian vortex) becomes hyperbolic fixed point in large-shell dynamics, producing recurrent reversals of mean pseudospin projection and repeated conversions between Laguerre-Gaussian vortex and Hermite-Gaussian multi-lobed transverse profiles.
AI.conclusion: Weak nonlinear magnetic entrance edges induce tennis-racket instability in twisted electron dynamics, with Lewis-Ermakov breathing modulating nonlinear strength and setting growth time scales; regime is accessible with standard octupole correctors in transmission electron microscopes.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Heterogeneous PDEs: The Neutron Diffusion Eigenvalue Problem
summary: We develop a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm to solve a type of linear reaction-diffusion equation, the neutron diffusion (generalized) k-eigenvalue problem that establishes nuclear criticality. The algorithm handles an equation with piecewise constant coefficients, describing a problem in a heterogeneous medium. We apply uniform finite elements and show that the quantum algorithm provides significant polynomial end-to-end speedup over its classical counterparts. This speedup leverages recent advances in quantum linear systems -- fast inversion and quantum preconditioning -- and uses Hamiltonian simulation as a subroutine. Our results suggest that quantum algorithms may provide speedups for heterogeneous PDEs, though the extent of this advantage over the fastest classical algorithm depends on the effectiveness of other classical approaches such as nonuniform or adaptive meshing for a given problem instance.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for neutron diffusion eigenvalue problems achieves polynomial speedup over classical methods using quantum linear system solvers and Hamiltonian simulation.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum algorithms for solving linear reaction-diffusion equations, specifically the neutron diffusion k-eigenvalue problem that determines nuclear criticality, aiming to achieve computational speedups for heterogeneous PDE problems.
AI.method: Hybrid classical-quantum algorithm using uniform finite elements, quantum linear system solvers (fast inversion and quantum preconditioning), and Hamiltonian simulation as a subroutine for piecewise constant coefficient equations in heterogeneous media.
AI.result: The quantum algorithm provides significant polynomial end-to-end speedup over classical counterparts, demonstrating quantum advantage for heterogeneous PDEs.
AI.conclusion: Quantum algorithms can provide speedups for heterogeneous PDEs, though the extent of advantage depends on classical approaches like nonuniform or adaptive meshing for specific problem instances.

title: A superconducting quantum circuit single artificial atom maser
summary: We demonstrate a circuit QED analog of an atomic micromaser that utilizes an artificial, multi level atom, pumped into a population-inverted state by a microwave tone, as the gain medium. Our demonstration is enabled by the flexibility of the circuit QED platform, which allowed us to precisely engineer the level-structure, coupling, and dissipation of the micromaser components. Our device shows rich physics and perhaps points to ways to use the recent developments in the domain of microwave quantum circuits to probe the domain of maser physics.

AI.tldr: Circuit QED implementation of an atomic micromaser using artificial multi-level atom as gain medium, enabled by precise engineering of quantum circuit components.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a circuit QED analog of an atomic micromaser, leveraging the flexibility of microwave quantum circuits to explore maser physics with engineered quantum systems.
AI.method: Utilizes an artificial multi-level atom (superconducting qubit/circuit) pumped into population-inverted state by microwave tone as gain medium; precise engineering of level-structure, coupling, and dissipation enabled by circuit QED platform flexibility.
AI.result: Successful demonstration of a circuit QED micromaser showing rich physics; points to new ways to use microwave quantum circuits for exploring maser physics.
AI.conclusion: Circuit QED platform enables precise engineering of micromaser components, demonstrating rich physics and opening pathways to probe maser physics using recent developments in microwave quantum circuits.

title: Quantum noise in ranging with optical pulses
summary: Optical frequency combs combine ultrashort pulse duration and phase stability, making them powerful resources for high-precision ranging even when affected by atmospheric dispersion. It has been established that by classical modal engineering and mdoe-sensitive detection sensitivity to distance at the standard limit can be achieved, however attaining improved uncertainties by the use of squeezing has not been explored. Here, we apply an effective Hamiltonian framework to the problem of ranging with quantum frequency combs in order to derive the associated precision bounds for distance estimation. We analyse the role of intensity anti-squeezing and temporal beam shaping, and find that quantum solutions may be appealing mostly for short-distance applications.

AI.tldr: Quantum frequency combs can achieve enhanced precision in short-distance ranging through squeezing and temporal beam shaping, though practical benefits over classical methods are limited to specific applications.
AI.motivation: While classical frequency combs achieve standard quantum limit precision in ranging, the potential for improved uncertainties using quantum squeezing techniques remains unexplored, motivating investigation of quantum frequency combs for enhanced distance estimation.
AI.method: Applied an effective Hamiltonian framework to analyze ranging with quantum frequency combs, deriving precision bounds for distance estimation while examining the roles of intensity anti-squeezing and temporal beam shaping.
AI.result: Quantum solutions show potential for improved precision in short-distance applications, with analysis revealing how squeezing and beam shaping affect distance estimation accuracy, though benefits over classical approaches are limited to specific scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Quantum frequency combs offer appealing precision advantages primarily for short-distance ranging applications, with intensity anti-squeezing and temporal beam shaping playing key roles in achieving enhanced measurement uncertainties.

title: In-Situ Simultaneous Magic State Injection on Arbitrary CSS qLDPC Codes
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can encode many logical qubits within a single code block at low physical qubit overhead, yet magic state injection into such codes remains largely underexplored. Existing state injection proposals for qLDPC codes predominantly follow an external prepare-and-transfer paradigm, in which raw magic states are prepared outside the target code block and subsequently injected via inter-code operations. We propose the first \emph{in-situ} magic state injection: a scheme in which logical magic states are directly prepared within a qLDPC memory block, only using resources required for syndrome extraction. We show that our scheme is generalizable to any CSS qLDPC code, with examples of circuit-level simulations on the $[[144,12,12]]$ Bivariate Bicycle (BB) code and the $[[225,9,4]]$ Hypergraph Product code. We focus on a regime where correlated injection errors are negligible. In the BB code, this corresponds to a configuration that simultaneously injects four logical $|Y\rangle$ states. Under a uniform depolarizing noise model with physical error rate $10^{-3}$, this achieves an injection error rate of $1.62 \times 10^{-3}$ per logical qubit, while the correlated-error contribution is only $2 \times 10^{-5}$ per logical qubit (about $1\%$ of the injection error rate). Under a hardware-motivated asymmetric noise model where single-qubit gate errors are $10\%$ of two-qubit gate errors, the injection error rate per logical qubit falls to $ 6.7 \times 10^{-4} $, below the error rate ($ 10^{-3} $) of the two-qubit gates used to encode the magic states. Its simplicity allows our scheme to be applied to arbitrary CSS qLDPC codes using only the ancilla qubits native to syndrome extraction, and yield a reduction in space overhead relative to both prepare-and-transfer approaches and surface-code-based magic state injection schemes.

AI.tldr: First in-situ magic state injection scheme for qLDPC codes that prepares logical magic states directly within the code block using only syndrome extraction resources, achieving low error rates and reduced space overhead.
AI.motivation: Magic state injection for qLDPC codes remains underexplored, with existing methods following external prepare-and-transfer paradigms that require separate preparation and inter-code operations. There's a need for more efficient, integrated approaches that leverage the native resources of qLDPC codes.
AI.method: Proposes an in-situ injection scheme where logical magic states are directly prepared within a qLDPC memory block using only resources required for syndrome extraction. The method is generalizable to any CSS qLDPC code, demonstrated with circuit-level simulations on the [[144,12,12]] Bivariate Bicycle code and [[225,9,4]] Hypergraph Product code.
AI.result: For the BB code with four logical |Y⟩ states under uniform depolarizing noise (p=10⁻³): injection error rate = 1.62×10⁻³ per logical qubit, correlated errors = 2×10⁻⁵ (∼1% of injection error). Under asymmetric noise (single-qubit errors = 10% of two-qubit errors): injection error rate = 6.7×10⁻⁴ per logical qubit, below the two-qubit gate error rate (10⁻³).
AI.conclusion: The in-situ scheme provides a simple, generalizable approach for magic state injection in CSS qLDPC codes using only native syndrome extraction ancillas, reducing space overhead compared to prepare-and-transfer methods and surface-code-based schemes while achieving competitive error rates.

title: Tight Quantum Lower Bound for k-Distinctness
summary:
In this paper, we introduce a new quantum query lower bound framework. It is inspired by Zhandry's compressed oracle technique, but it also subsumes the polynomial method as a special case. Compared to Zhandry's technique, our approach has two key differences. First, we do not use any oracles (except for the standard input oracle), and define ``knowledge'' directly through the expansion of the state of the algorithm in the Fourier basis. Second, we allow arbitrary probability distributions of inputs.
  We show how this framework behaves on the problem of finding equal elements in the input string. In particular, we demonstrate its power by proving a first tight quantum query lower bound for the k-Distinctness problem.

AI.tldr: New quantum query lower bound framework combining compressed oracle technique and polynomial method, enabling tight lower bounds for k-Distinctness problem.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum query lower bound techniques have limitations. Zhandry's compressed oracle technique is powerful but has constraints, while the polynomial method is a special case. There's a need for a more general framework that can handle arbitrary input distributions and provide tight bounds for important problems like k-Distinctness.
AI.method: Develops a new quantum query lower bound framework inspired by Zhandry's compressed oracle technique but without using oracles (except standard input oracle). Defines "knowledge" directly through Fourier basis expansion of algorithm states. Allows arbitrary probability distributions of inputs. Combines strengths of compressed oracle technique and polynomial method.
AI.result: Demonstrates framework's effectiveness on finding equal elements in input strings. Proves first tight quantum query lower bound for the k-Distinctness problem, showing the framework's power and generality.
AI.conclusion: The new framework provides a powerful tool for quantum query complexity analysis, unifying and extending previous techniques while enabling tight lower bounds for important problems previously unattainable with existing methods.

title: Star product for qubit states in phase space and star exponentials
summary: In this paper, we formulate the phase space description of qubit systems using coadjoint orbits of $SU(2)$ and the Stratonovich-Weyl correspondence, yielding a deformation quantization on the sphere. The resulting star product reproduces the operator algebra of complexified quaternions and its antisymmetric part induces the Lie-Poisson structure associated with the Kirillov-Kostant-Souriau symplectic form. We show that quantum dynamics can be expressed entirely in phase space through star exponentials of Hamiltonian symbols, leading to an explicit representation of the propagator. Further, we establish the equivalence between the coherent-state path integral formulation on $S^2$ and the algebraic description in terms of star exponentials. Some examples illustrating the construction of the star-exponential functions and the resulting Poisson structure are included.

AI.tldr: Phase space description of qubit systems using SU(2) coadjoint orbits and Stratonovich-Weyl correspondence yields deformation quantization on sphere with star product reproducing complexified quaternion algebra.
AI.motivation: To formulate a phase space description of qubit systems that connects geometric quantization methods with operator algebra, enabling quantum dynamics to be expressed entirely in phase space.
AI.method: Uses coadjoint orbits of SU(2) and Stratonovich-Weyl correspondence to perform deformation quantization on the sphere, constructing star products that reproduce complexified quaternion operator algebra and induce Lie-Poisson structure.
AI.result: Quantum dynamics can be expressed through star exponentials of Hamiltonian symbols, providing explicit propagator representation; equivalence established between coherent-state path integral on S² and algebraic star-exponential description.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a complete phase space formulation for qubit systems connecting geometric quantization, operator algebra, and path integral methods through deformation quantization on SU(2) coadjoint orbits.

title: Quantum Hilbert Space Fragmentation and Entangled Frozen States
summary: We find that rank deficiency of the local Hamiltonian in a classically fragmented model is the key mechanism leading to quantum Hilbert space fragmentation. The rank deficiency produces local null directions that can generate entangled frozen states (EFS): entangled states embedded in mobile classical Krylov sectors that do not evolve under Hamiltonian dynamics. When the entangled frozen subspace is non-empty, the mobile classical sector splits into an mobile quantum Krylov subspace and an entangled frozen subspace, and the model exhibits quantum fragmentation. We establish this mechanism in four models of increasing symmetry structure: an asymmetric qubit projector with no symmetry, the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric GHZ projector, a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-symmetric cyclic qutrit projector, and the Temperley-Lieb model. For the asymmetric and GHZ projector models, we obtain closed-form expressions for irreducible Krylov dimensions, degeneracies, and sector multiplicities. Further, we introduce the notion of weak and strong quantum fragmentation, the quantum counterpart of the weak-strong distinction in classical fragmentation. After removing the EFS, the mobile quantum Krylov subspace decomposes into irreducible blocks. In the weak case, the number of irreducible blocks remains $\mathcal{O}(1)$, each is individually ergodic with Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) level statistics, and the unresolved spectrum follows an $m$GOE distribution. In the strong case, the number of irreducible blocks grows with system size, and the gap-ratio distribution approaches Poisson as $L\to\infty$.

AI.tldr: Rank deficiency in classically fragmented Hamiltonians creates local null directions that generate entangled frozen states, leading to quantum Hilbert space fragmentation with mobile quantum Krylov subspaces and entangled frozen subspaces.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism behind quantum Hilbert space fragmentation, specifically how rank deficiency of local Hamiltonians in classically fragmented models leads to the emergence of entangled frozen states and quantum fragmentation.
AI.method: Analysis of rank deficiency producing local null directions that generate entangled frozen states (EFS). Study of four models with increasing symmetry: asymmetric qubit projector (no symmetry), Z₂-symmetric GHZ projector, Z₃-symmetric cyclic qutrit projector, and Temperley-Lieb model. Introduction of weak vs. strong quantum fragmentation classification.
AI.result: For asymmetric and GHZ projector models, obtained closed-form expressions for irreducible Krylov dimensions, degeneracies, and sector multiplicities. Identified that after removing EFS, mobile quantum Krylov subspace decomposes into irreducible blocks with different statistical properties: weak fragmentation shows O(1) blocks with GOE statistics, strong fragmentation shows growing number of blocks with Poisson statistics as system size increases.
AI.conclusion: Rank deficiency of local Hamiltonian in classically fragmented models is the key mechanism leading to quantum Hilbert space fragmentation through creation of entangled frozen states, with distinct weak and strong fragmentation regimes characterized by different spectral statistics.

title: Square-root Time Atom Reconfiguration Plan for Lattice-shaped Mobile Tweezers
summary: This paper proposes a scalable planning algorithm for creating defect-free atom arrays in neutral-atom systems. The algorithm generates a $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt N)$ time plan for $N$ atoms by parallelizing atom transport using a two-dimensional lattice pattern generated by acousto-optic deflectors. Our approach is based on a divide-and-conquer strategy that decomposes an arbitrary reconfiguration problem into at most three one-dimensional shuttling tasks, enabling each atom to be transported with a total transportation cost of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt N)$. Using the Gale--Ryser theorem, the proposed algorithm provides a highly reliable solution for arbitrary target geometries. We further introduce a peephole optimization technique that improves reconfiguration efficiency for grid target geometries. Numerical simulations on a 632$\times$632 atom array demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves a grid configuration plan that reduces the total transportation cost to 1/7 of state-of-the-art algorithms, while resulting in 32%--35% more atom captures. We believe that our scalability improvement contributes to realizing large-scale quantum computers based on neutral atoms. Our experimental code is available from https://github.com/kotamanegi/sqrt-time-atom-reconfigure.

AI.tldr: Scalable O(√N) time planning algorithm for defect-free atom arrays using parallel transport via acousto-optic deflectors and divide-and-conquer strategy.
AI.motivation: Need for scalable planning algorithms to create defect-free atom arrays in neutral-atom quantum computing systems, addressing the challenge of efficiently reconfiguring large numbers of atoms.
AI.method: Divide-and-conquer strategy decomposing arbitrary reconfiguration into at most three 1D shuttling tasks, using Gale-Ryser theorem for reliable solutions, acousto-optic deflectors for parallel transport, and peephole optimization for grid geometries.
AI.result: Achieves 1/7 reduction in total transportation cost compared to state-of-the-art algorithms, with 32-35% more atom captures in 632×632 atom array simulations.
AI.conclusion: The algorithm's scalability improvement contributes to realizing large-scale quantum computers based on neutral atoms by enabling efficient defect-free array creation.

title: Addressing a device in a quantum network: A quantum approach including routing
summary: In this work we propose an addressing scheme for quantum networks which relies on quantum states held by devices. Quantum network devices use their address state together with a request state that encodes the tasks to be executed. Our approach not only removes the necessity to classically communicate addresses, but also the need to communicate the operations a device must apply. It turns out that utilizing entanglement to encode addresses of devices in a quantum network leads to interesting applications such as overlaying different network states. We present a distributed quantum routing protocol using entanglement that coherently selects a route in a network of Bell-states for controlled-teleportation and lastly we prove that addressing using quantum states is equivalent to performing tasks in superposition in a quantum network.

AI.tldr: Quantum addressing scheme using quantum states instead of classical communication for network routing and task execution
AI.motivation: To eliminate the need for classical communication of addresses and operations in quantum networks by using quantum states for addressing
AI.method: Proposes a quantum addressing scheme where devices use quantum address states with request states encoding tasks; utilizes entanglement to encode device addresses; presents distributed quantum routing protocol using entanglement for coherent route selection in Bell-state networks
AI.result: Enables interesting applications like overlaying different network states; demonstrates quantum routing for controlled-teleportation; proves equivalence between quantum state addressing and performing tasks in superposition
AI.conclusion: Quantum addressing using quantum states provides fundamental advantages over classical approaches, enabling superposition-based network operations and eliminating classical communication overhead

title: Noise is not always detrimental: the capacity of quantum batteries is enhanced in black holes
summary: Quantum battery capacity, as a critical metric for quantifying energy storage and release in quantum systems, exhibits complex behaviors in curved spacetime and noisy environments. This study focuses on bipartite mixed state, aiming to explore the modulation of quantum battery capacity by Hawking radiation and environmental noise. We find a counterintuitive phenomenon that Hawking radiation can enhance battery capacity, exerting a positive influence on energy storage, a result that stands in stark contrast to the detrimental effects typically associated with entanglement and coherence. When a quantum battery is simultaneously subjected to environmental noise and Hawking radiation, its capacity generally degrades, with the extent of degradation depending on the type of noise. The charging and discharging behaviors largely follow the same patterns observed in the noiseless scenario; however, under a bit flip channel with strong noise intensity, the charging-discharging pattern reverses. In the extreme case of maximum noise intensity, the capacity of the quantum battery under depolarizing noise tends to zero. The underlying physical mechanism lies in the fact that the bit flip channel disrupts the original population distribution of energy levels, thereby altering the average energy of the system and establishing a perturbative environment for bidirectional energy exchange. This differs fundamentally from the phase flip channel. These findings offer a new perspective for the theory of quantum batteries in noninertial reference frames.

AI.tldr: Hawking radiation can surprisingly enhance quantum battery capacity in curved spacetime, while environmental noise generally degrades it, with bit flip channels causing charging-discharging pattern reversal and depolarizing noise driving capacity to zero at maximum intensity.
AI.motivation: To investigate how quantum battery capacity is modulated by Hawking radiation and environmental noise in curved spacetime, particularly focusing on the counterintuitive effects of Hawking radiation on energy storage in bipartite mixed states.
AI.method: Analysis of bipartite mixed state quantum batteries in curved spacetime, examining the effects of Hawking radiation and various types of environmental noise (bit flip, phase flip, depolarizing channels) on battery capacity, charging, and discharging behaviors.
AI.result: Hawking radiation enhances quantum battery capacity (positive effect), contrasting with typical detrimental effects on entanglement/coherence. Environmental noise generally degrades capacity, with degradation dependent on noise type. Bit flip channels with strong noise intensity reverse charging-discharging patterns. Depolarizing noise at maximum intensity drives capacity to zero. Bit flip channels disrupt population distribution of energy levels, altering average energy and creating bidirectional energy exchange environment.
AI.conclusion: Hawking radiation can positively impact quantum battery capacity, while environmental noise effects depend on noise type, with bit flip channels fundamentally different from phase flip channels in their mechanisms. These findings provide new perspectives for quantum battery theory in noninertial reference frames.

title: Dynamics of Entanglement in Schwarzschild Black Holes
summary: To characterize the effect of Hawking radiation induced by the quantum atmosphere beyond the event horizon on entanglement, we employ concurrence as the entanglement measure for a bipartite mixed state and investigate its evolution with Hawking temperature. We find that the physically accessible concurrence decreases as the Hawking acceleration increases, whereas the physically inaccessible concurrence exhibits the opposite behavior, increasing monotonically from zero. We further establish several trade-off relations on concurrence, revealing its distribution between physically accessible and inaccessible regions. Additionally, we study the dynamics of concurrence under three types of channel noise. The results indicate that the evolution of concurrence depends on the specific noise channel: unlike the phase damping channel, sudden death of concurrence occurs in both phase flip and bit flip channels, the concurrence exhibits a certain symmetry with respect to the noise parameter during its evolution under bit flip channel noise.

AI.tldr: Study of Hawking radiation's effect on quantum entanglement using concurrence measure, showing entanglement redistribution between accessible/inaccessible regions and different noise channel behaviors.
AI.motivation: To characterize how Hawking radiation from the quantum atmosphere beyond the event horizon affects quantum entanglement, specifically investigating entanglement evolution with Hawking temperature and under different noise channels.
AI.method: Employ concurrence as entanglement measure for bipartite mixed states, analyze evolution with Hawking temperature, establish trade-off relations between physically accessible and inaccessible concurrence, and study dynamics under three types of channel noise (phase damping, phase flip, bit flip).
AI.result: Physically accessible concurrence decreases with increasing Hawking acceleration, while physically inaccessible concurrence increases monotonically from zero. Trade-off relations reveal entanglement distribution between regions. Under noise: concurrence evolution depends on channel type - sudden death occurs in phase flip and bit flip channels but not phase damping; bit flip channel shows symmetry with respect to noise parameter.
AI.conclusion: Hawking radiation redistributes entanglement between physically accessible and inaccessible regions, with different noise channels exhibiting distinct entanglement dynamics including sudden death phenomena in certain channels.

title: Molecular Excited States using Quantum Subspace Methods: Accuracy, Resource Reduction, and Error-Mitigated Hardware Implementation of q-sc-EOM
summary: Problems in quantum chemical simulations, especially achieving accurate excited-state potential energy surfaces, are among the primary applications to achieve quantum utility. On near-term quantum hardware, variants of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms are the primary choice for chemistry simulation. In this study, a combination of leading ground and excited state quantum algorithms for general excited states, namely, ADAPT-VQE/LUCJ and q-sc-EOM, are utilized to calculate accurate excited state potential energy surfaces in challenging bond-breaking scenarios and compared with the classical scalable EOM-CCSD method. This work investigates avenues toward quantum utility in excited-state quantum chemistry using the q-sc-EOM approach. We assess its accuracy while mitigating major scaling bottlenecks through the Davidson algorithm and basis rotation grouping, reducing the measurement scaling from O(N$^{12}$) to O(N$^{5}$), and implementing the method on quantum hardware with various error mitigation strategies to reduce gate and measurement errors in excited states. The hardware implementation of the q-sc-EOM algorithm, augmented by mitigation of M3 readout error and symmetry projection, produces reasonably accurate excited-state energies with gate noise identified as the predominant source of error. This paves the way for accurate and scalable, generally applicable quantum excited-state methods with potential for quantum utility while identifying critical problems that require advancements.

AI.tldr: Combination of ADAPT-VQE/LUCJ and q-sc-EOM algorithms for accurate excited-state potential energy surfaces on quantum hardware, with scaling improvements from O(N¹²) to O(N⁵) and error mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: Achieving quantum utility in quantum chemistry requires accurate excited-state potential energy surfaces, especially for challenging bond-breaking scenarios, using near-term quantum hardware where VQE variants are the primary choice.
AI.method: Combined ADAPT-VQE/LUCJ for ground states with q-sc-EOM for excited states, implemented with Davidson algorithm and basis rotation grouping to reduce measurement scaling from O(N¹²) to O(N⁵), plus hardware error mitigation including M3 readout error mitigation and symmetry projection.
AI.result: Hardware implementation with error mitigation produces reasonably accurate excited-state energies, with gate noise identified as the main error source; scaling improvements enable practical implementation while maintaining accuracy comparable to classical EOM-CCSD.
AI.conclusion: The q-sc-EOM approach paves the way for accurate, scalable quantum excited-state methods with potential for quantum utility, though gate noise remains a critical challenge requiring further advancements.

title: Granularity Noise Limit in Atomic-Ensemble-Based Metrology
summary: Conventional noise analysis in atomic-ensemble sensing assumes a continuous-medium approximation, thereby treating the atomic system as a deterministic dielectric. Here, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down due to the discrete, particulate nature of the ensemble, giving rise to an intrinsic "atomic granularity noise" (AGN) that fundamentally competes with the optical measurement noise (OMN, typically photon shot noise). By introducing a discrete-atom statistical framework, we derive a unified noise-scaling law governed by a single dimensionless resource ratio, $\mathcal{R} = \bar{N}_{\mathrm{ph}}/\bar{N}_{\mathrm{at}}$ at (the photon-to-atom flux ratio). This law predicts a continuous crossover from an OMN-limited regime to an AGN-limited regime. Crucially, our results reveal a counter-intuitive constraint for sensor optimization: increasing optical probe power -- standard practice to mitigate OMN -- can paradoxically degrade sensitivity by driving the system into the AGN-dominated regime. Furthermore, we identify a critical resource threshold, $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{crit}}$, beyond which quantum-enhanced metrology using non-classical light fails to improve sensitivity, as it becomes limited by the AGN.

AI.tldr: Atomic ensembles in sensing exhibit intrinsic 'atomic granularity noise' from discrete atom nature, competing with optical measurement noise, with unified scaling law based on photon-to-atom flux ratio revealing counter-intuitive optimization constraints.
AI.motivation: Conventional noise analysis treats atomic ensembles as continuous deterministic dielectrics, ignoring the discrete particulate nature that creates intrinsic atomic granularity noise competing with optical measurement noise.
AI.method: Introduce discrete-atom statistical framework to derive unified noise-scaling law governed by dimensionless resource ratio R = photon-to-atom flux ratio, analyzing crossover between OMN-limited and AGN-limited regimes.
AI.result: Derived scaling law predicts continuous crossover from OMN-limited to AGN-limited regimes, revealing counter-intuitive constraint: increasing optical probe power can degrade sensitivity by driving system into AGN-dominated regime, and identifying critical resource threshold beyond which quantum-enhanced metrology fails.
AI.conclusion: Atomic granularity noise fundamentally limits atomic-ensemble sensing, imposing constraints on sensor optimization and quantum-enhanced metrology, requiring careful consideration of photon-to-atom flux ratio rather than simply increasing probe power.

title: Decoherence-induced Multiphoton Interference
summary: Decoherence is usually deemed detrimental to quantum information processing. Its control and minimization require significant costs and operating overheads, constituting a major hurdle to commercialize quantum technology. Yet, quantum mechanics provides for counterintuitive, sometimes surprisingly useful, phenomena and effects associated with decoherence, leading to unusual practical utilities. Here we demonstrate such an example of fundamental interest and practical potential, where genuine quantum interference is created among multiple photons through their dissipative coupling to a shared reservoir. On a thin-film lithium niobate chip, we incoherently link two spontaneous parametric down-converters through a common, highly-lossy channel to create coherent multiphoton states. Our results show that faithful correlations can be established among two, three, and four photons, and tuned by shifting the relative phase between the driving pumps for the converters. This experiment highlights an under-explored territory in quantum science and technology, where loss and decoherence serve as resources, rather than adversaries, for quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Researchers demonstrate that decoherence and loss can be used as resources to create coherent multiphoton states through dissipative coupling to a shared reservoir, enabling quantum interference among multiple photons.
AI.motivation: Decoherence is typically considered detrimental to quantum information processing, requiring costly control and minimization. This work explores counterintuitive phenomena where decoherence can be useful, aiming to demonstrate practical utilities of dissipative quantum effects.
AI.method: Using a thin-film lithium niobate chip, two spontaneous parametric down-converters are incoherently linked through a common, highly-lossy channel. The dissipative coupling to a shared reservoir creates coherent multiphoton states, with correlations tuned by shifting the relative phase between driving pumps.
AI.result: The experiment successfully demonstrates faithful correlations among two, three, and four photons. Quantum interference is created among multiple photons through dissipative coupling, and correlations can be tuned by adjusting the relative phase between converter pumps.
AI.conclusion: This work highlights an under-explored territory where loss and decoherence serve as resources rather than adversaries for quantum information processing, demonstrating fundamental interest and practical potential of dissipative quantum effects.

title: A Digital Spreading Framework for Quantum Expectation Computation Without Rotation Gates or Arithmetic Circuits
summary: In the pursuit of quantum advantage for financial engineering, researchers face a critical dilemma: analog rotation gates suffer from inherent 'sine-to-square' biases and error magnification, while digital arithmetic circuits (e.g., WeightedAdder) incur prohibitive quadratic complexity that exceeds NISQ capabilities. This study introduces Digital Spreading (DS), a fully digital quantum computing framework designed to resolve this trade-off. DS overcomes these limitations by utilizing a pruned Cuccaro ripple-carry architecture that avoids costly multiplication and eliminates rotation gates entirely. The proposed circuit employs integer comparison operations on superposed quantum states, mapping multi-qubit outcomes onto the probability of a single target qubit. Experiments based on a random walk model for option pricing demonstrate that DS achieves floating-point precision with a relative error as low as 0.0001%, outperforming JP Morgan's rotation-based method (1.43%), as well as ITRI's analog calibration (1.43%) and digital calibration approaches (19.14%). Overall, DS provides a compact, robust, and accurate framework for quantum weighted-average computation.

AI.tldr: Digital Spreading (DS) is a fully digital quantum computing framework that eliminates rotation gates and reduces quadratic complexity, achieving floating-point precision with 0.0001% relative error for option pricing.
AI.motivation: Current quantum approaches for financial engineering face a critical dilemma: analog rotation gates suffer from inherent 'sine-to-square' biases and error magnification, while digital arithmetic circuits incur prohibitive quadratic complexity that exceeds NISQ capabilities.
AI.method: DS uses a pruned Cuccaro ripple-carry architecture that avoids costly multiplication and eliminates rotation gates entirely. The circuit employs integer comparison operations on superposed quantum states, mapping multi-qubit outcomes onto the probability of a single target qubit.
AI.result: Experiments based on a random walk model for option pricing demonstrate that DS achieves floating-point precision with relative error as low as 0.0001%, outperforming JP Morgan's rotation-based method (1.43%), ITRI's analog calibration (1.43%), and digital calibration approaches (19.14%).
AI.conclusion: DS provides a compact, robust, and accurate framework for quantum weighted-average computation, resolving the trade-off between analog and digital approaches for quantum advantage in financial engineering.

title: Another Triumph of Locality: Colliding Histories Skew Handshakes
comment: 16 pages. Forthcoming in 'Bold Conjectures, Volume II: Essays Across Physics', edited by Logan Chipkin, Conjecture Press, 2026
summary: From gravity to electromagnetism, apparent action at a distance has always been resolved by deeper, local explanations. Yet today, Bell's theorem is widely interpreted as the death knell for local reality. In this chapter, I present the theorem in accessible terms, examine the three main strategies that attempt to preserve hidden variables, and argue that they share a common defect: the attempt to explain the quantum from the classical rather than the other way around. In unitary quantum mechanics, classicality itself is given a quantum account, and, when the Bell scenario is formulated in the Heisenberg picture, a strictly local explanation emerges. This chapter serves as a non-technical front-end to 'Explaining Bell Locally' (Proc. R. Soc. A).

AI.tldr: Bell's theorem challenges local realism, but a quantum explanation in the Heisenberg picture reveals strict locality when classicality is understood as emergent from quantum mechanics.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to challenge the widespread interpretation of Bell's theorem as disproving local reality, arguing that conventional approaches mistakenly try to explain quantum phenomena from classical perspectives rather than understanding classicality as emergent from quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The author presents Bell's theorem in accessible terms, examines three main strategies attempting to preserve hidden variables, and argues these approaches share a common defect. The key methodological innovation is formulating the Bell scenario in the Heisenberg picture of unitary quantum mechanics, where classicality receives a quantum account.
AI.result: When the Bell scenario is properly formulated in the Heisenberg picture, a strictly local explanation emerges, demonstrating that apparent non-locality arises from trying to explain quantum phenomena through classical frameworks rather than understanding classicality as quantum-emergent.
AI.conclusion: Bell's theorem does not disprove local reality when properly understood through quantum mechanics. The apparent non-locality stems from the mistaken attempt to explain quantum phenomena from classical perspectives; when classicality is understood as emergent from quantum mechanics (particularly in the Heisenberg picture), a strictly local explanation becomes possible.

title: Phase-Fidelity-Aware Truncated Quantum Fourier Transform for Scalable Phase Estimation on NISQ Hardware
summary: Quantum phase estimation~(QPE) is central to numerous quantum algorithms, yet its standard implementation demands an $\calO(m^{2})$-gate quantum Fourier transform~(QFT) on $m$ control qubits-a prohibitive overhead on near-term noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We introduce the \emph{Phase-Fidelity-Aware Truncated QFT} (PFA-TQFT), a family of approximate QFT circuits parameterised by a truncation depth~$d$ that omits controlled-phase rotations below a hardware-calibrated fidelity threshold~$\eps$. Our central result establishes $\TV(P_{\varphi},P_{\varphi}^{d})\leqπ(m{-}d)/2^{d}$, showing that for $d=\calO(\log m)$ circuit size collapses from $\calO(m^{2})$ to $\calO(m\log m)$ while estimation error grows by at most $\calO(2^{-d})$. We characterise $\dstar=\Floor{\log_{2}(2π/\eps_{2q})}$ directly from native gate fidelities, demonstrating 31.3 -43.7\% at m = 30, gate-count reduction on IBM Eagle/Heron and IonQ~Aria with negligible accuracy loss. Numerical experiments on the transverse-field Ising model confirm all theoretical predictions and reveal a \emph{noise-truncation synergy}: PFA-TQFT outperforms full QFT under NISQ noise $\eps_{2q}\gtrsim 2\times10^{-3}$.

AI.tldr: PFA-TQFT reduces QPE circuit size from O(m²) to O(m log m) by truncating low-fidelity controlled-phase rotations, achieving significant gate-count reductions on NISQ hardware with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Standard QPE requires O(m²)-gate QFT on m control qubits, which is prohibitive on near-term NISQ devices due to noise and limited coherence times.
AI.method: Phase-Fidelity-Aware Truncated QFT (PFA-TQFT) - a family of approximate QFT circuits parameterized by truncation depth d that omits controlled-phase rotations below a hardware-calibrated fidelity threshold ε.
AI.result: Theoretical bound: TV(P_φ, P_φ^d) ≤ π(m-d)/2^d; for d = O(log m), circuit size collapses from O(m²) to O(m log m) with estimation error O(2^-d). Achieves 31.3-43.7% gate-count reduction at m=30 on IBM/IonQ hardware. Numerical experiments on transverse-field Ising model confirm predictions and reveal noise-truncation synergy where PFA-TQFT outperforms full QFT under NISQ noise ε_2q ≳ 2×10^-3.
AI.conclusion: PFA-TQFT enables practical QPE on NISQ devices by dramatically reducing circuit complexity while maintaining accuracy, with the added benefit of noise-truncation synergy that makes it outperform full QFT in noisy environments.

title: Non-Markovian exceptional points in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, to appear in Advanced Quantum Technologies (Wiley)
summary: Spontaneous emission of a quantum emitter, such as an excited atom, is a fundamental process in quantum electrodynamics (QED), typically associated with exponential decay to the ground state accompanied by irreversible photon emission. This simple Markovian picture, however, is profoundly modified in the presence of time-delayed feedback, structured continua, or cooperative emission, as occurs when an emitter radiates in front of a mirror, when several emitters radiate collectively, or in the case of a giant atom. In such regimes, strong non-Markovian dynamics arise from photon reabsorption and interference effects, leading to pronounced deviations from exponential decay. Here we demonstrate the emergence of exceptional points (EPs) in these highly non-Markovian waveguide-QED environments, i.e., non-Markovian EPs. These EPs appear directly in the relaxation dynamics as sharp transitions to oscillatory behavior, manifested by the appearance of real zeros in the excited-state amplitude. We analyze in detail the spontaneous emission of giant atoms with two or more coupling points, highlighting the mechanisms leading to non-Markovian EPs, and show that similar phenomena arise in other waveguide-QED settings, such as the collective spontaneous emission of spatially separated point-like emitters. Our results reveal waveguide-QED systems as experimentally accessible platforms for realizing and exploring non-Markovian EP physics.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates the emergence of exceptional points (EPs) in non-Markovian waveguide-QED environments, showing how strong non-Markovian dynamics from photon reabsorption and interference lead to sharp transitions to oscillatory behavior in spontaneous emission.
AI.motivation: Traditional Markovian descriptions of spontaneous emission fail in waveguide-QED systems with time-delayed feedback, structured continua, or cooperative emission. These non-Markovian regimes exhibit complex dynamics that require new theoretical frameworks to understand phenomena like exceptional points in quantum decay processes.
AI.method: The authors analyze spontaneous emission of giant atoms with multiple coupling points to waveguide modes, examining the relaxation dynamics and identifying conditions where exceptional points emerge. They extend their analysis to other waveguide-QED settings including collective spontaneous emission of spatially separated point-like emitters.
AI.result: The study reveals that non-Markovian exceptional points appear as sharp transitions to oscillatory behavior in relaxation dynamics, manifested by real zeros in the excited-state amplitude. These EPs emerge from the interplay of photon reabsorption and interference effects in waveguide-QED environments.
AI.conclusion: Waveguide-QED systems provide experimentally accessible platforms for realizing and exploring non-Markovian exceptional point physics, offering new insights into quantum decay processes beyond traditional Markovian descriptions.

title: Qurator: Scheduling Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows Across Heterogeneous Cloud Providers
summary: As quantum computing moves from isolated experiments toward integration with large-scale workflows, the integration of quantum devices into HPC systems has gained much interest. Quantum cloud providers expose shared devices through first-come first-serve queues where a circuit that executes in 3 seconds can spend minutes to an entire day waiting. Minimizing this overhead while maintaining execution fidelity is the central challenge of quantum cloud scheduling, and existing approaches treat the two as separate concerns. We present Qurator, an architecture-agnostic quantum-classical task scheduler that jointly optimizes queue time and circuit fidelity across heterogeneous providers. Qurator models hybrid workloads as dynamic DAGs with explicit quantum semantics, including entanglement dependencies, synchronization barriers, no-cloning constraints, and circuit cutting and merging decisions, all of which render classical scheduling techniques ineffective. Fidelity is estimated through a unified logarithmic success score that reconciles incompatible calibration data from IBM, IonQ, IQM, Rigetti, AQT, and QuEra into a canonical set of gate error, readout fidelity, and decoherence terms. We evaluate Qurator on a simulator driven by four months of real queue data using circuits from the Munich Quantum Toolkit benchmark suite. Across load conditions from 5 to 35,000 quantum tasks, Qurator stays within 1% of the highest-fidelity baseline at low load while achieving 30-75% queue time reduction at high load, at a fidelity cost bounded by a user-specified target.

AI.tldr: Qurator is a quantum-classical task scheduler that jointly optimizes queue time and circuit fidelity across heterogeneous quantum cloud providers by modeling hybrid workloads as dynamic DAGs with quantum semantics and using a unified fidelity estimation framework.
AI.motivation: Quantum cloud providers use first-come first-serve queues where circuits can wait minutes to days despite short execution times. Existing approaches treat queue time minimization and execution fidelity as separate concerns, creating a need for joint optimization.
AI.method: Qurator models hybrid workloads as dynamic DAGs with explicit quantum semantics (entanglement dependencies, synchronization barriers, no-cloning constraints, circuit cutting/merging decisions). It uses a unified logarithmic success score to reconcile incompatible calibration data from multiple providers into canonical gate error, readout fidelity, and decoherence terms.
AI.result: Evaluation on a simulator with four months of real queue data using Munich Quantum Toolkit benchmarks shows Qurator stays within 1% of highest-fidelity baseline at low load while achieving 30-75% queue time reduction at high load, with fidelity cost bounded by user-specified target.
AI.conclusion: Qurator successfully addresses the central challenge of quantum cloud scheduling by jointly optimizing queue time and circuit fidelity across heterogeneous providers, demonstrating significant performance improvements while maintaining fidelity constraints.

title: Quantum state determinability from local marginals is universally robust
summary: A fundamental problem in quantum physics is to establish whether a multiparticle quantum state can be uniquely determined from its local marginals. In theory, this problem has been addressed in the exact case where the marginals are perfectly known. In practice, however, experiments only have access to finite statistics and therefore can only determine the marginals of a quantum state up to an error. In this Letter, we prove that unique determinability universally survives such local imperfections: specifically, for every uniquely determined state, we show that deviations of local marginals propagate to global states strictly bounded by a power law with exponent $α\in(0,1]$. This result induces a classification of multipartite quantum states by their power-law exponents, with linear scaling $α=1$ as the most favorable regime. We derive a necessary and sufficient criterion for linear robustness and translate it into an executable semidefinite-programming certification. Applying our theory, we prove that stabilizer states are inherently square-root robust and provide a complete robustness classification for the Dicke family. Finally, we exploit these results to construct a scalable two-local genuine multipartite entanglement witness, demonstrating the viability of this framework for broad practical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that quantum state uniqueness from local marginals remains robust under finite statistics, with deviations propagating via power-law scaling, enabling classification by robustness exponents and practical certification methods.
AI.motivation: While quantum state uniqueness from local marginals is theoretically solved for perfect knowledge, practical experiments only access finite statistics, creating uncertainty about whether uniqueness survives such local imperfections.
AI.method: Prove that unique determinability universally survives local imperfections by showing deviations of local marginals propagate to global states via power-law scaling. Derive necessary and sufficient criterion for linear robustness and translate it into semidefinite-programming certification. Apply theory to analyze robustness of stabilizer states and Dicke states.
AI.result: Established that for every uniquely determined state, local marginal deviations propagate to global states with power-law scaling (exponent α∈(0,1]). Stabilizer states are inherently square-root robust (α=1/2). Complete robustness classification for Dicke family. Constructed scalable two-local genuine multipartite entanglement witness.
AI.conclusion: Unique determinability of quantum states from local marginals is robust to finite statistics, enabling practical certification and classification by power-law exponents. The framework supports broad applications including scalable entanglement witnessing.

title: Resource Implications of Different Encodings for Quantum Computational Fluid Dynamics
summary: For quantum algorithms for problems in which the task is to compute an entire field of values, like e.g. computational fluid dynamics (CFD), it is often proposed amplitude encoding w.r.t. multiple qubits; however, the efforts implied by it for initialization and read-out are not addressed. This work is devoted specifically to this issue: It reviews different encoding schemes in quantum computing, discussing their computational costs for initialization and read-out as well as resulting aspects for their usage via minimal examples. The considerations in previous literature on the required computational resources for amplitude encoding w.r.t. multiple qubits are extended in the presented quantification by explicitly deducing the circuit depth that results for the decomposed initialization procedure of V. V. Shende et al. [1, 2] and deriving an upper bound for the necessary number of executions of a quantum algorithm to extract the encoded values with a specific accuracy. For these two results, an empirical verification via the means provided by IBM's quantum computing simulation framework $\textit{Qiskit}$ [3] is given. In the framework of the study on the required number of runs to achieve a desired accuracy, it is however found that the derived upper bound, scaling like $ {\tilde{n}^2} ~ {\ln( {\tilde{n}} )} $ with the number of encoded values $ {\tilde{n}} $, is too conservative to be used for precise estimations. Therefore, a corresponding study of the required runs for the reference distribution of equal probabilities for all basis states is done in particular, which suggests $ {\tilde{n}} ~ { \ln( {\tilde{n}} ) } $ as an empirical scaling law. Since the view regarding CFD applications is taken here, it is presented in particular that the insights from this work lead to a new encoding approach, which is proposed specifically for a quantum algorithm for the lattice Boltzmann method.

AI.tldr: Analysis of computational costs for amplitude encoding in quantum algorithms, focusing on initialization/read-out overhead, with empirical verification and application to CFD/lattice Boltzmann methods.
AI.motivation: Address the overlooked computational costs of amplitude encoding for multi-qubit quantum algorithms in field-value problems like CFD, particularly initialization and read-out overhead.
AI.method: Review encoding schemes, quantify circuit depth for Shende's initialization decomposition, derive upper bound for required executions to extract encoded values with accuracy, and empirically verify using Qiskit.
AI.result: Derived upper bound scales as ñ²ln(ñ) but found too conservative; empirical study suggests ñln(ñ) scaling for equal probability distributions; proposed new encoding approach for lattice Boltzmann method.
AI.conclusion: Amplitude encoding for multi-qubit systems has significant initialization/read-out costs; empirical scaling laws provide practical guidance; new encoding scheme proposed for CFD applications, specifically lattice Boltzmann methods.

title: PQC-Enhanced QKD Networks: A Layered Approach
