summary: We present a layered and modular network architecture that combines Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) to provide scalable end-to-end security across long distance multi-hop, trusted-node quantum networks. To ensure interoperability and efficient practical deployment, hop-wise tunnels between physically secured nodes are protected by WireGuard with periodically rotated pre-shared keys sourced via the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface. On top, Rosenpass performs a PQC key exchange to establish an end-to-end data channel without modifying deployed QKD devices or network protocols. This dual-layer composition yields post-quantum forward secrecy and authenticity under practical assumptions. We implement the design using open-source components and validate and evaluate it in simulated and lab test-beds. Experiments show uninterrupted operation over multi-hop paths, low resource footprint and fail-safe mechanisms. We further discuss the design's compositional security, wherein the security of each individual component is preserved under their combination and outline migration paths for operators integrating QKD-aware overlays in existing infrastructures.

AI.tldr: A layered network architecture combining QKD and PQC for scalable end-to-end security in multi-hop quantum networks, using WireGuard for hop-wise tunnels and Rosenpass for end-to-end PQC key exchange.
AI.motivation: To provide scalable end-to-end security across long distance multi-hop quantum networks while ensuring interoperability and practical deployment, addressing the need for post-quantum forward secrecy and authenticity in quantum network infrastructures.
AI.method: A dual-layer modular architecture: 1) Hop-wise tunnels between physically secured nodes protected by WireGuard with periodically rotated pre-shared keys via ETSI GS QKD 014 interface; 2) Rosenpass performing PQC key exchange on top to establish end-to-end data channels without modifying existing QKD devices or protocols.
AI.result: Successful implementation using open-source components with validation in simulated and lab test-beds showing uninterrupted operation over multi-hop paths, low resource footprint, and fail-safe mechanisms. The design achieves post-quantum forward secrecy and authenticity under practical assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The layered QKD-PQC architecture provides scalable end-to-end security for multi-hop quantum networks while preserving individual component security through compositional design, offering practical migration paths for operators integrating quantum-aware overlays into existing infrastructures.

title: A solid-state quantum memory based on a continuous optoacoustic system
summary: Quantum memories for optical states are essential resources for quantum communication and information processing. We propose a quantum memory protocol based on coherent photon-phonon transduction in a Brillouin-active optical waveguide supporting traveling acoustic modes. A pulsed pump drives an effective beam-splitter interaction between optical and acoustic fields, enabling the mapping of a propagating optical quantum state onto a traveling phononic excitation and its subsequent retrieval on demand. Using a continuum optoacoustic model, we show that the protocol enables broadband quantum state storage in a distributed medium without relying on discrete cavity modes. Analytical and numerical results demonstrate high-fidelity storage and retrieval of squeezed and entangled states under experimentally realistic parameters. The memory bandwidth is set by the Brillouin interaction and can reach hundreds of MHz. Our results identify continuum Brillouin optomechanical systems as a scalable platform for broadband quantum memories and multimode quantum signal processing.

AI.tldr: Proposal of a broadband quantum memory protocol using Brillouin optomechanics in optical waveguides for coherent photon-phonon transduction, enabling storage and retrieval of quantum states without discrete cavity modes.
AI.motivation: Quantum memories for optical states are essential for quantum communication and information processing, but current approaches often rely on discrete cavity modes with limited bandwidth.
AI.method: Protocol based on coherent photon-phonon transduction in Brillouin-active optical waveguides using pulsed pump-driven beam-splitter interactions between optical and acoustic fields, analyzed with continuum optoacoustic models.
AI.result: Analytical and numerical results demonstrate high-fidelity storage and retrieval of squeezed and entangled states with bandwidths reaching hundreds of MHz under experimentally realistic parameters.
AI.conclusion: Continuum Brillouin optomechanical systems provide a scalable platform for broadband quantum memories and multimode quantum signal processing without reliance on discrete cavity modes.

title: Loss-aware state space geometry for quantum variational algorithms
summary: The natural gradient descent optimisation technique is an efficient optimising protocol for broad classes of classical and quantum systems that takes the underlying geometry of the parameter manifold into account by means of using either the Fisher information metric of the classical probability distribution function or the Fubini-Study tensor of the associated parametrised quantum states in the consequent update rules. Even though the natural gradient descent procedure utilises the geometry of the space of probability or states, it is, however, insensitive to the measure of parametrised distance on the space of possible outcomes when the corresponding optimising problem is considered for the expectation value of a classical or quantum observable with respect to the probability distribution or the quantum state. In this work, we introduce a generic optimising principle, where the intrinsic geometry of the space of outcomes has been taken into account suitably, either by using an ambient space construction with a base statistical manifold with the usual Fisher information metric (or the Fubini-Study tensor), where the loss hypersurface is embedded to, or by means of a first-principle construction from the overlap of nearby quantum states on the projective Hilbert space. This construction as well as a family of conformal variants yields a form of loss-aware natural gradient updates that rescale the effective step size while preserving the descent direction. We benchmark the resulting optimisers on variational quantum circuit examples and on a classical neural network task, finding that, while the standard natural gradient remains the most robust on average, the proposed conformal schemes can improve best-case convergence in favourable regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel optimization principle that incorporates the geometry of outcome spaces, extending natural gradient descent to account for loss function geometry through ambient space embeddings or quantum state overlaps.
AI.motivation: Standard natural gradient descent considers the geometry of parameter spaces (via Fisher information or Fubini-Study metric) but ignores the geometry of outcome spaces when optimizing expectation values. This limitation motivates developing optimization methods that account for both parameter and outcome space geometries.
AI.method: Two approaches: 1) Ambient space construction embedding loss hypersurfaces into statistical manifolds with Fisher/Fubini-Study metrics, and 2) First-principle construction using quantum state overlaps on projective Hilbert space. Both yield loss-aware natural gradient updates with conformal variants that rescale step sizes while preserving descent directions.
AI.result: Benchmarking on variational quantum circuits and classical neural networks shows standard natural gradient remains most robust on average, but proposed conformal schemes can improve best-case convergence in favorable regimes.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully develops optimization methods that incorporate outcome space geometry, providing loss-aware natural gradient updates that can enhance convergence in specific scenarios while maintaining the robustness of standard approaches.

title: Estimation of trace distance between two arbitrary quantum states
summary: When it comes to discriminating between two quantum states, trace distance is one of the well-known metrics used in quantum computation and quantum information theory. While there are several quantum algorithms for calculating the trace distance between two quantum states, computing it for any two general density matrices remains computationally demanding. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm based on the exponentiation of the density matrix and the improved quantum phase estimation (IQPE) to determine the trace distance for both pure and mixed states, with a time complexity of $O(N^8)$ where $N$ is the number of qubits of the given states. We demonstrate its ability to predict the quantity with proof-of-principle simulations and also quantum hardware computations on the IBM quantum computers, confirming its promise for near-term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm using density matrix exponentiation and improved quantum phase estimation to compute trace distance between quantum states with O(N⁸) complexity, validated on IBM quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Trace distance is fundamental in quantum information theory but computationally demanding to compute for general density matrices, especially on near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: Proposes quantum algorithm combining density matrix exponentiation with improved quantum phase estimation (IQPE) to compute trace distance for both pure and mixed states.
AI.result: Algorithm achieves O(N⁸) time complexity where N is number of qubits, demonstrated through proof-of-principle simulations and quantum hardware computations on IBM quantum computers.
AI.conclusion: The algorithm shows promise for near-term quantum devices, providing an efficient method for trace distance computation in quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Learning of Classical Correlations with continuous-domain Pauli Correlation Encoding
summary: We propose a quantum machine learning framework for estimating classical covariance matrices using parameterized quantum circuits within the Pauli-Correlation-Encoding (PCE) paradigm. We introduce two quantum covariance estimators: the C-Estimator, which constructs the covariance matrix through a Cholesky factorization to enforce positive (semi)definiteness, and a computationally efficient E-Estimator, which directly estimates covariance entries from observable expectation values. We analyze the trade-offs between the two estimators in terms of qubit requirements and learning complexity, and derive sufficient conditions on regularization parameters to ensure positive (semi)definiteness of the estimators. Furthermore, we show that the barren plateau phenomenon in training the variational quantum circuit for E-estimator can be mitigated by appropriately choosing the regularization parameters in the loss function for HEA ansatz. The proposed framework is evaluated through numerical simulations using randomly generated covariance matrices. We examine the convergence behavior of the estimators, their sensitivity to low-rank assumptions, and their performance in covariance completion with partially observed matrices. The results indicate that the proposed estimators provide a robust approach for learning covariance matrices and offer a promising direction for applying quantum machine learning techniques to high-dimensional statistical estimation problems.

AI.tldr: Quantum machine learning framework for classical covariance matrix estimation using parameterized quantum circuits with two estimators: C-Estimator (Cholesky-based) and E-Estimator (direct expectation-based), analyzing trade-offs and mitigating barren plateaus.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum machine learning techniques for high-dimensional statistical estimation problems, specifically for learning classical covariance matrices, which are fundamental in many statistical and machine learning applications.
AI.method: Proposes a quantum machine learning framework within the Pauli-Correlation-Encoding (PCE) paradigm using parameterized quantum circuits. Introduces two estimators: C-Estimator constructs covariance matrix through Cholesky factorization to enforce positive (semi)definiteness; E-Estimator directly estimates covariance entries from observable expectation values. Analyzes trade-offs in qubit requirements and learning complexity, derives sufficient conditions for regularization parameters to ensure positive (semi)definiteness, and shows how to mitigate barren plateaus in variational quantum circuits for E-Estimator.
AI.result: Numerical simulations with randomly generated covariance matrices show the estimators provide robust approach for learning covariance matrices. Examined convergence behavior, sensitivity to low-rank assumptions, and performance in covariance completion with partially observed matrices. Demonstrated that barren plateau phenomenon can be mitigated by appropriately choosing regularization parameters in loss function for HEA ansatz.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum covariance estimators offer a promising direction for applying quantum machine learning techniques to high-dimensional statistical estimation problems, with robust performance in covariance matrix learning and completion tasks.

title: Coherence and Imaginarity as Resources in Quantum Circuit Complexity
summary: Quantum circuit complexity quantifies the minimal number of gates needed to realize a unitary transformation and plays a central role in quantum computation. In this work, we investigate the complexity of quantum circuits through coherence and imaginarity resources. We establish a lower bound on the circuit cost by the Tsallis relative $α$ entropy of cohering power, which is shown to be tighter than the one presented by Bu et al.[\textit{Communications in Mathematical Physics} 405, no. 7 (2024):161] under restrictive conditions. As a consequence, we obtain the relationships between the circuit cost and the coherence generating power via probabilistic average in terms of skew information/relative entropy, and present explicit bounds of the circuit cost for typical quantum gates. Moreover, we derive lower bounds on the circuit cost via the imaginaring power of the circuit, induced by the Tsallis relative $α$ entropy and relative entropy. We demonstrate that imaginarity can yield nontrivial constraints on the circuit cost even when coherence-based lower bounds are zero (e.g., for the $T$ gate), which implies that imaginarity may provide advantages under certain circumstances compared with coherence. Our results may help better understand the connections between quantum resources and circuit complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes new lower bounds on quantum circuit complexity using coherence and imaginarity resources, showing tighter bounds than previous work and demonstrating that imaginarity provides nontrivial constraints even when coherence-based bounds are zero.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit complexity is fundamental to quantum computation, but existing bounds may not be tight. The authors aim to develop better lower bounds using quantum resource theories (coherence and imaginarity) to understand the connections between quantum resources and circuit complexity.
AI.method: The authors use Tsallis relative α entropy to establish lower bounds on circuit cost via cohering power. They derive relationships between circuit cost and coherence generating power through probabilistic averages using skew information/relative entropy. They also derive bounds via imaginarity power using Tsallis relative α entropy and relative entropy.
AI.result: The paper presents tighter lower bounds than Bu et al. (2024) under restrictive conditions, explicit bounds for typical quantum gates, and demonstrates that imaginarity yields nontrivial constraints even when coherence-based bounds are zero (e.g., for the T gate).
AI.conclusion: Imaginarity provides advantages over coherence in certain circumstances for bounding circuit complexity, offering new insights into the connections between quantum resources and circuit complexity.

title: The final version of a recent approach towards quantum foundation
summary: In several articles, this author has advocated an alternative approach towards quantum foundation based upon a set of postulates, and based upon the notions of theoretical variables and of accessible theoretical variables. It is shown in this article that this basis can be considerably simplified. In particular, the assumption that there exists an inaccessible variable $φ$ such that all the accessible ones can be seen as functions of $φ$, can be dropped. This assumption has been difficult to motivate in the previous articles. From this, I get a simple basis for the main Theorems.The essential assumption is that there in the given context exist two different maximal accessible variables, what Niels Bohr would have called two complementary variables. From this, the whole Hilbert space formalism may be derived. It is also discussed in some detail how this Hilbert space should be chosen. The resulting theory is a purely mathematical theory, but it leads to qunantum mechanics by letting the variables be physical variables. Other applications of the main theory are also considered. The mathematical proofs are mostly deferred to the Appendix.

AI.tldr: The author simplifies their previous quantum foundations framework by eliminating the need for an inaccessible variable φ, instead basing the theory on the existence of two complementary maximal accessible variables, from which the entire Hilbert space formalism can be derived.
AI.motivation: To simplify and strengthen the author's previous approach to quantum foundations by eliminating the problematic assumption of an inaccessible variable φ that was difficult to motivate, while still deriving quantum mechanics from a more natural starting point.
AI.method: The author develops a purely mathematical theory based on theoretical variables and accessible theoretical variables, starting from the essential assumption that there exist two different maximal accessible variables (complementary variables in Bohr's terminology). From this foundation, the Hilbert space formalism is derived, and the paper discusses how to appropriately choose the Hilbert space.
AI.result: The author obtains a simplified basis for their main theorems, showing that the entire Hilbert space formalism can be derived from the existence of two complementary maximal accessible variables, without needing the previously required inaccessible variable φ. The resulting theory can be applied to quantum mechanics by interpreting the variables as physical variables.
AI.conclusion: The author presents a more streamlined foundation for quantum mechanics that eliminates the problematic inaccessible variable assumption, instead building the theory on the natural concept of complementary variables, which leads to the full Hilbert space formalism and can be applied to quantum mechanics and other domains.

title: A plug-and-play superconducting quantum controller at millikelvin temperatures enables exceeding 99.9% average gate fidelity
summary: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computing requires efficient in-situ control methods that allow high-fidelity operations at millikelvin temperatures. Superconducting circuits based on Josephson junctions offer a promising solution due to their high speed, low power dissipation, and cryogenic nature. Here, we report a superconducting quantum controller that enables direct chip-to-chip interconnection with qubits at 10 mK and high-fidelity, all-digital manipulation. Randomized benchmarking reveals a uniformly high average Clifford fidelity of 99.9% with leakage to high energy levels on the order of $10^{-4}$, and an estimated average gate operation energy of 0.121 fJ, demonstrating the potential to resolve the control bottleneck in superconducting quantum computing.

AI.tldr: Superconducting quantum controller enables high-fidelity (99.9%) digital manipulation of qubits at 10 mK with low energy consumption (0.121 fJ/gate), addressing control bottleneck in large-scale quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Large-scale superconducting quantum computing requires efficient in-situ control methods at millikelvin temperatures to overcome the control bottleneck, as traditional room-temperature control electronics face challenges in scalability, power dissipation, and signal integrity.
AI.method: Developed a superconducting quantum controller using Josephson junction-based superconducting circuits that enables direct chip-to-chip interconnection with qubits at 10 mK, featuring all-digital manipulation capabilities and cryogenic operation.
AI.result: Randomized benchmarking demonstrated uniformly high average Clifford fidelity of 99.9% with leakage to high energy levels on the order of 10⁻⁴, and estimated average gate operation energy of 0.121 fJ per gate.
AI.conclusion: The superconducting quantum controller successfully addresses the control bottleneck in superconducting quantum computing by providing high-fidelity, low-energy, cryogenic control that enables scalable quantum processor architectures.

title: Mirror Dual Symmetry in Physics
comment: Invited article for the Special Issue Focus on Quantum Rabi Models: After 90 Years and Into the Future
summary: The quantum Rabi model has been a useful and pedagogical quantum model in the past decades, sufficiently simple to be solved analytically and intuitively understood, while sufficiently complex as to provide highly non-trivial eigenstates and a practical description of quantum optical platforms for quantum technologies. The Dirac equation, especially when restricted to 1+1 dimensions, is a simple toy model as well, but its easy diagonalization enabled historically to connect the electron spin to the fermionic statistics, among others. Both models share a symmetry at the purely mathematical level, namely, the spectra of each one has a dual equivalent under energy sign change, that I name a mirror dual symmetry. Usually, one quantizes these equations by assuming a ground state energy for the bosonic mode. But there is another option for the interpretation of the Hamiltonian, as I will argue, that is to assume a total symmetry principle, namely, that the total energy is zero at all times, for either the quantum Rabi model or the Dirac equation, and impose the constraint that every positive energy excitation has a mirror excitation of negative energy. This possibility, which was, apparently, ignored in the times when Paul Dirac was studying the implications of his equation, would avoid the worries in the scientific community that the negative energy solutions would decay until minus infinity, thus obviating the necessity to build a highly artificial Dirac sea, and instead impose what has always been successful in Physics, which is the enforcement of symmetry principles. Assuming a total symmetry principle, many of the problems of current Physics, such as renormalization of quantum gravity, dark matter, and dark energy, may possibly be automatically solved. One obvious result would be the automatic cancellation of the zero point energy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes interpreting quantum models (Rabi and Dirac) with a total symmetry principle where total energy is zero, eliminating negative energy decay problems and potentially solving fundamental physics issues.
AI.motivation: To address the problematic interpretation of negative energy solutions in quantum models (particularly Dirac equation) that historically required artificial constructs like the Dirac sea, and to explore whether enforcing symmetry principles could resolve fundamental physics problems.
AI.method: Reinterprets quantum Rabi model and Dirac equation by assuming a total symmetry principle where total energy is zero at all times, imposing that every positive energy excitation has a mirror negative energy excitation, thus avoiding the need for Dirac sea.
AI.result: The proposed interpretation would eliminate worries about negative energy solutions decaying to minus infinity, obviate the need for Dirac sea, automatically cancel zero point energy, and potentially solve problems like quantum gravity renormalization, dark matter, and dark energy.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing symmetry principles (total energy zero with mirror dual symmetry) in quantum models could provide a more natural framework that automatically resolves long-standing problems in physics without artificial constructs.

title: Kinetic Uncertainty Relation in Collective Dissipative Quantum Many-Body Systems
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures; 8 pages of supplementary material with 1 figure
summary: Attaining the ultimate precision remains a central objective in the engineering of nanoscale systems and the investigation of nonequilibrium processes. While thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations establish fundamental precision bounds, prior derivations in the quantum regime have remained confined to single-body systems. Consequently, the ultimate precision limits for interacting many-body systems have been unknown. In this Letter, we analytically formulate a kinetic uncertainty relation for a many-body system undergoing collective dissipation, a paradigmatic model of boundary time crystals. By applying a mean-field approximation, we derive lower bounds for relative fluctuations expressed in terms of clear physical quantities. Our analysis identifies a cooperative enhancement mechanism, demonstrating that collective interactions allow the precision to scale with the number of particles. We validate these findings through numerical simulations across the stationary, critical, and boundary time crystal phases. Our work presents the first theoretical description of precision bounds in collective dissipative quantum many-body systems for an arbitrary particle number $N$, providing a solid foundation for designing future quantum technologies that exploit many-body phenomena.

AI.tldr: First derivation of precision bounds for interacting many-body quantum systems undergoing collective dissipation, revealing cooperative enhancement where precision scales with particle number.
AI.motivation: While thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations establish fundamental precision bounds in quantum systems, previous derivations were limited to single-body systems, leaving the ultimate precision limits for interacting many-body systems unknown.
AI.method: Analytically formulate a kinetic uncertainty relation for a many-body system with collective dissipation (paradigmatic model of boundary time crystals), apply mean-field approximation to derive lower bounds for relative fluctuations expressed in terms of clear physical quantities.
AI.result: Identifies cooperative enhancement mechanism where collective interactions allow precision to scale with the number of particles; validated through numerical simulations across stationary, critical, and boundary time crystal phases.
AI.conclusion: First theoretical description of precision bounds in collective dissipative quantum many-body systems for arbitrary particle number N, providing foundation for designing future quantum technologies exploiting many-body phenomena.

title: A Nested Amplitude Amplification Protocol for the Binary Knapsack Problem
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Amplitude Amplification offers a provable speedup for search problems, which is leveraged in combinatorial optimization by Grover Adaptive Search (GAS). The protocol demands deep circuits that are challenging with regards to NISQ capabilities. We propose a nested Amplitude Amplification protocol for the binary knapsack problem that splits the decision tree at a tunable depth, performing a partial amplification on the first variables before executing a global GAS on the full search space. The partial amplification is implemented by an Inner Iteration Finder that selects the rotation count maximizing marked-subspace amplitude. The resulting biased superposition serves as the initial state for the outer Amplitude Amplification. Using the Quantum Tree Generator for feasible-state preparation and an efficient classical amplitude-tracking scheme, we simulate the protocol on knapsack instances of sizes intractable by statevector simulation. Our results show that the nested approach reduces the cost of improving an incumbent solution compared to baseline GAS, particularly for a specific subset of knapsack instances. As combinatorial problems in domains such as semiconductor supply-chain planning grow in scale, methods that reduce circuit cost are an important step toward eventual quantum advantage for such applications.

AI.tldr: Nested Amplitude Amplification protocol for binary knapsack reduces quantum circuit depth by splitting decision tree, performing partial amplification on first variables before global Grover Adaptive Search, enabling simulation of larger instances.
AI.motivation: Amplitude Amplification provides quantum speedup for search problems but requires deep circuits challenging for NISQ devices; combinatorial optimization problems like knapsack need reduced circuit costs for practical quantum advantage.
AI.method: Nested Amplitude Amplification protocol splits decision tree at tunable depth, uses Inner Iteration Finder for partial amplification on first variables to create biased superposition, then performs global GAS on full search space with Quantum Tree Generator for state preparation.
AI.result: Nested approach reduces cost of improving incumbent solutions compared to baseline GAS, particularly for specific knapsack instances, enabling simulation of sizes intractable by statevector simulation.
AI.conclusion: Methods reducing circuit cost are crucial step toward quantum advantage for large-scale combinatorial problems like semiconductor supply-chain planning; nested amplification offers practical improvement over standard GAS.

title: Quantum-Boosted Nonlinear Tunneling Driven by a Bright Squeezed Vacuum
comment: This is the initial submission; revised submission will be available upon approval
summary: Nonlinear processes, mediated by multiphoton interactions rather than single-photon response, drive numerous fundamental phenomena and momentous applications in modern physics. Among these processes, tunneling ionization plays a pivotal role as it drives high-harmonic generation, forming the basis of attosecond science and enabling the visualization and control of electron motion at its natural time scale. Quantum light, with its unique capacity for quantum noise redistribution, offers a transformative solution to boost nonlinear responses. Here, we report the first experiment of nonlinear tunneling ionization of the most fundamental system of atoms boosted by a quantum light -- bright squeezed vacuum (BSV). Remarkably, the tunneling ionization of a single sodium atom induced by a 300 nJ BSV beam matches that achieved with a 7.1 {\textmu}J coherent light source, demonstrating a dramatic boost in nonlinear efficiency from phase-squeezed quantum light. Moreover, the effective intensity of the BSV light and thus the boosted tunneling ionization can be precisely controlled by tuning the degree of phase squeezing while maintaining the average pulse energy. These findings provide fundamental insights into quantum-boosted nonlinear effect and pave the way for efficient frequency conversion and quantum-controlled molecular reactions using tailored quantum light sources.

AI.tldr: Quantum light (bright squeezed vacuum) dramatically boosts tunneling ionization efficiency compared to coherent light, enabling strong nonlinear effects with much lower pulse energies.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum light with quantum noise redistribution can significantly enhance nonlinear processes like tunneling ionization, which is fundamental to attosecond science and electron dynamics control.
AI.method: Experimental comparison of tunneling ionization in single sodium atoms using bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) versus coherent light sources, with precise control of phase squeezing while maintaining average pulse energy.
AI.result: Tunneling ionization induced by 300 nJ BSV matches that achieved with 7.1 μJ coherent light, showing ~24x boost in nonlinear efficiency; effective intensity can be controlled by tuning phase squeezing degree.
AI.conclusion: Quantum light provides fundamental insights into quantum-boosted nonlinear effects and enables efficient frequency conversion and quantum-controlled molecular reactions using tailored quantum light sources.

title: Deviations from thermal light statistics in ensembles of independent two-level emitters
summary: We investigate the light statistics of an ensemble of independent motionless two-level atoms in a product state. We identify the conditions under which the cold atomic ensemble emits thermal light statistics characterized by the Gaussian Moment Theorem. For the theorem to hold, we derive for each correlation order two conditions on the atom number and the ratio of coherent to incoherent light emission. We further discuss their validity for atoms either in a pure or mixed state. Our results contribute to the understanding of the generation of thermal light by two-level atoms without interactions among the emitters.

AI.tldr: Independent motionless two-level atoms in product states can emit thermal light with Gaussian statistics under specific conditions on atom number and coherent/incoherent emission ratio.
AI.motivation: To understand how thermal light statistics can emerge from an ensemble of non-interacting two-level atoms, specifically identifying the conditions under which Gaussian (thermal) statistics occur despite the atoms being independent and in product states.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of light statistics from an ensemble of independent motionless two-level atoms. Derivation of conditions for Gaussian Moment Theorem to hold at each correlation order, considering both atom number and ratio of coherent to incoherent emission. Examination of validity for atoms in pure versus mixed states.
AI.result: For each correlation order, two specific conditions are derived: one on the atom number and one on the ratio of coherent to incoherent light emission. These conditions determine when the atomic ensemble emits thermal light with Gaussian statistics. The analysis shows these conditions apply to both pure and mixed atomic states.
AI.conclusion: Thermal light statistics can be generated by independent two-level atoms without interactions when specific conditions on atom number and coherent/incoherent emission ratio are satisfied, providing insight into how Gaussian statistics emerge from non-interacting quantum emitters.

title: Quantum optomechanics of lossy bodies: general approach and structured squeezed vacuum effects
summary: We investigate the overall optomechanical force experienced by a macroscopic lossy object in free space under external quantum illumination. To this end, utilizing the Modified Langevin Noise Formalism (MLNF), we derive the time-averaged expectation value of the Maxwell stress tensor for a non-equilibrium scenario in which the incoming scattering field is prepared in an arbitrary mixed quantum state, while the medium-assisted field is maintained in local thermal equilibrium. In the limit of full radiation-matter thermal equilibrium, our expression exactly recovers the well-known fluctuation-dissipation relation governing the Casimir effect, and, under coherent illumination, it yields the standard classical radiation pressure. We demonstrate that by driving the scattering field with an anisotropic, multimode squeezed vacuum state, the spatial profile of the electromagnetic quantum fluctuations can be engineered to exhibit broken rotational symmetry, thereby inducing a purely quantum mechanical force acting on the object. Such mechanical interaction is generated in the strict absence of a mean field, $\langle\hat{\mathbf{E}}\rangle=0$, and its non-classical nature is evidenced by its reliance on second-order field correlations $\langle\hat{\mathbf{E}}^2\rangle$, unlike classical optical radiation pressure governed by the squared mean field $\langle\hat{\mathbf{E}}\rangle^2$. Applying this exact formulation to a homogeneous lossy sphere, we demonstrate the experimental feasibility of the effect using realistic material parameters and optical estimations. Ultimately, we establish a general formalism for macroscopic quantum optomechanics that operates beyond the constraints of thermal equilibrium, enabling the prediction of regimes where the purely quantum force circumvents classical mean fields and shot noise while preserving the object's macroscopic quantum coherence.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum optomechanical formalism for calculating forces on macroscopic objects under arbitrary quantum illumination, showing that anisotropic squeezed vacuum states can generate purely quantum mechanical forces without classical mean fields.
AI.motivation: To establish a general quantum optomechanical framework that operates beyond thermal equilibrium constraints, enabling prediction of purely quantum forces on macroscopic objects that circumvent classical radiation pressure and shot noise while preserving quantum coherence.
AI.method: Utilizes Modified Langevin Noise Formalism (MLNF) to derive time-averaged expectation value of Maxwell stress tensor for non-equilibrium scenarios with arbitrary mixed quantum states for incoming scattering fields while maintaining medium-assisted fields in local thermal equilibrium.
AI.result: Derived expression recovers Casimir effect fluctuation-dissipation relation in full thermal equilibrium and classical radiation pressure under coherent illumination. Shows anisotropic multimode squeezed vacuum states can engineer broken rotational symmetry in quantum fluctuations, generating purely quantum mechanical forces without mean fields (⟨Ê⟩=0). Applied to homogeneous lossy sphere with realistic parameters demonstrates experimental feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Established general macroscopic quantum optomechanics formalism enabling prediction of regimes where purely quantum forces circumvent classical mean fields and shot noise while preserving macroscopic quantum coherence, opening new possibilities for quantum control of macroscopic objects.

title: Fault-Tolerant One-Shot Entanglement Generation with Constant-Sized Quantum Devices in the Plane
summary: Consider a rectangular grid of qubits in 2D with single-qubit and nearest-neighbor two-qubit operations subject to local stochastic Pauli noise. At different length scales, this setup describes both a single quantum computing device with geometrically limited connectivity between qubits arranged on a disc, and planar networks composed of quantum repeater stations of constant size. We give a protocol which robustly generates entanglement between distant qubits in this setup. For noise below a constant threshold error strength, it generates a constant-fidelity Bell pair between qubits separated by an arbitrarily large distance $R$. To generate distance-$R$ entanglement, a rectangular grid of qubits of dimensions $Θ(R)\times Θ(\mathsf{poly}(\log R))$ suffices. Our protocol applies quantum operations in one shot, establishing a Bell state in a constant time up to a known Pauli correction. In contrast, existing entanglement generation protocols either require local quantum devices controlling a number of qubits growing with the targeted distance, or are not single-shot, i.e., have a distance-dependent execution time. The protocol leverages many-body entanglement in networks and provides the first example of a short-range entangled state in 2D with long-range localizable entanglement robust to local stochastic Pauli noise. As an immediate corollary, we construct a 2D-local stabilizer Hamiltonian whose Gibbs states possess long-range localizable entanglement at constant positive temperature.

AI.tldr: Protocol generates long-distance entanglement in 2D qubit grids with local Pauli noise using constant-sized devices and constant time, enabling robust Bell pairs across arbitrary distances.
AI.motivation: Existing entanglement generation protocols either require device size scaling with distance or have distance-dependent execution times. There's a need for single-shot protocols using constant-sized local devices that work robustly against local noise.
AI.method: Uses a rectangular grid of qubits with dimensions Θ(R)×Θ(poly(log R)) and applies quantum operations in one shot. Leverages many-body entanglement in networks to create short-range entangled states in 2D with long-range localizable entanglement robust to local stochastic Pauli noise.
AI.result: For noise below a constant threshold, the protocol generates constant-fidelity Bell pairs between qubits separated by arbitrarily large distance R in constant time (up to known Pauli correction). Provides first example of robust long-range localizable entanglement in 2D with local noise.
AI.conclusion: The protocol enables practical long-distance entanglement generation using constant-sized quantum devices, with applications to quantum computing devices with limited connectivity and quantum repeater networks. As corollary, constructs 2D-local stabilizer Hamiltonian with long-range localizable entanglement at constant positive temperature.

title: Dynamical decoupling and quantum error correction with SU(d) symmetries
summary: Dynamical decoupling is a long-established and effective way to suppress unwanted interactions in qubit systems, enabling advances in fields ranging from quantum metrology to quantum computing. For general qudit systems, however, comparable protocols remain rare, mainly because Hamiltonian engineering in higher dimensions lacks the geometric intuition available for qubits. Here we present a general framework for dynamical decoupling in qudit systems, based on Lie group representation theory. By extending the group theory approach to dynamical decoupling, we show how decoupling groups can be systematically identified among the finite subgroups of SU(d) by analyzing their access to the irreducible components of the operator space. As an application, we construct new pulse sequences for interacting qutrit systems based on finite subgroups of SU(3), and show how subgroup factorizations and group orientations can be exploited to obtain shorter and more experimentally practical protocols for spin-1 systems with large zero-field splitting. We further show that the same symmetry-based framework yields quantum error-correcting codes: whenever a finite subgroup of SU(d) acts as a decoupling group for the relevant error algebra, the associated one-dimensional symmetry sectors define codespaces satisfying the Knill-Laflamme conditions, thereby unifying dynamical decoupling and quantum error correction in multi-level quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A general framework for dynamical decoupling in qudit systems using Lie group representation theory, enabling systematic identification of decoupling groups and unifying dynamical decoupling with quantum error correction.
AI.motivation: Dynamical decoupling protocols for qudit systems remain rare due to lack of geometric intuition in higher dimensions, despite their effectiveness in qubit systems for suppressing unwanted interactions in quantum technologies.
AI.method: Extends group theory approach to dynamical decoupling using Lie group representation theory; analyzes finite subgroups of SU(d) to identify decoupling groups by examining their access to irreducible components of operator space; constructs pulse sequences for qutrit systems using finite subgroups of SU(3).
AI.result: Developed systematic framework for qudit dynamical decoupling; constructed new pulse sequences for interacting qutrit systems; showed how subgroup factorizations and orientations yield shorter, more practical protocols for spin-1 systems; demonstrated that the same framework yields quantum error-correcting codes when finite subgroups act as decoupling groups.
AI.conclusion: The symmetry-based framework unifies dynamical decoupling and quantum error correction in multi-level quantum systems, providing a systematic approach for qudit systems that was previously lacking due to geometric limitations in higher dimensions.

title: Adaptive Deformation of Color Code in Square Lattices with Defects
summary: Quantum error correction is a crucial technology for fault tolerant quantum computing. On superconducting platforms, hardware defects in large scale quantum processors can disrupt the regular lattice structure of topological codes and impair their error correction capabilities. Although defect adaptive methods for surface codes have been extensively studied, other topological codes such as color codes still lack a systematic framework for handling defects. To address this issue, we propose a universal superstabilizer scheme applicable to data qubit defects in arbitrary stabilizer codes. Based on this scheme, we develop concrete repair methods for isolated defects of both internal data qubits and ancilla qubits in color codes defined on square lattices. Furthermore, for ancilla qubit defects, we present two optimization schemes. One scheme reuses neighboring ancilla qubits, and the other employs iSWAP gates. Unlike conventional approaches that directly disable neighboring data qubits and thus cause resource waste, both of our schemes avoid such waste and consequently achieve a lower logical error rate.Integrating the above techniques, we construct a comprehensive defect adaptive architecture for color codes to handle various defect clusters. We also show that our scheme supports a full transversal Clifford gate set and lattice surgery operations. These results provide a systematic theoretical pathway for deploying robust and low overhead color codes on defective quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: A universal superstabilizer scheme for handling data qubit defects in arbitrary stabilizer codes, with concrete repair methods for color codes that avoid resource waste and achieve lower logical error rates.
AI.motivation: Hardware defects in superconducting quantum processors disrupt the regular lattice structure of topological codes like color codes, impairing error correction capabilities. While defect adaptive methods exist for surface codes, color codes lack a systematic framework for handling defects.
AI.method: Proposes a universal superstabilizer scheme applicable to data qubit defects in arbitrary stabilizer codes. Develops concrete repair methods for isolated defects of internal data qubits and ancilla qubits in color codes on square lattices. For ancilla qubit defects, presents two optimization schemes: one reuses neighboring ancilla qubits, and the other employs iSWAP gates.
AI.result: Both optimization schemes avoid resource waste compared to conventional approaches that disable neighboring data qubits, achieving lower logical error rates. The comprehensive defect adaptive architecture handles various defect clusters and supports full transversal Clifford gate set and lattice surgery operations.
AI.conclusion: Provides a systematic theoretical pathway for deploying robust and low-overhead color codes on defective quantum hardware, addressing a critical gap in quantum error correction for topological codes beyond surface codes.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithm for Hamiltonian Simulation
summary: We introduce a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for simulating a Hamiltonian of the form $H= \sum_{i=1}^K H_i = \sum_{i=1}^K H_{i_1} \otimes H_{i_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes H_{i_M}$. Given that the entries of all $\{ H_{i_1}, H_{i_2} , \cdots , H_{i_M}\}$ (for all $i$) are classically known, we present a procedure (with three variants) in which these operators are classically diagonalized, and then this information is fed into three possible quantum procedures to obtain the block-encoding of $H$. The evolution operator $\exp(-iHt)$ is then obtained using the standard block-encoding/quantum singular value transformation framework. In the case where $\{H_i\}_{i=1}^K$ commute pairwise, our method can be trivially extended to the case with time-dependent coefficients. We provide a detailed discussion of the efficient regime of our hybrid framework and compare it with existing quantum simulation algorithms. Our algorithm can serve as a useful complement to existing quantum simulation algorithms, thereby expanding the reach of quantum computers for practically simulating physical systems. As a side contribution, we will show how the recent technique called \textit{randomized truncation to a quantum state} developed by Harrow, Lowe, and Witteveen [arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.08518, 2025] can be applied to the context of quantum simulation and particularly quantum state preparation, for which the latter can be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: A hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for Hamiltonian simulation using classical diagonalization of tensor product operators and quantum block-encoding, with extensions to time-dependent commuting Hamiltonians and applications of randomized truncation techniques.
AI.motivation: To develop a complementary quantum simulation method that leverages classical computational resources for diagonalizing known Hamiltonian components, expanding the practical reach of quantum computers for simulating physical systems with structured Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Three variants of a hybrid procedure: classical diagonalization of tensor product operators {H_i1, H_i2, ..., H_iM}, feeding this information into quantum procedures to obtain block-encoding of H, then using standard block-encoding/quantum singular value transformation framework for evolution operator exp(-iHt). Extends to time-dependent coefficients for commuting Hamiltonians.
AI.result: A detailed discussion of the efficient regime of the hybrid framework and comparison with existing quantum simulation algorithms, showing it serves as a useful complement to expand quantum simulation capabilities. Includes application of randomized truncation technique to quantum simulation and state preparation.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid algorithm provides a practical approach to quantum simulation by combining classical diagonalization with quantum block-encoding, particularly useful for structured Hamiltonians with known tensor product components, expanding the applicability of quantum computers for physical system simulation.

title: Quantum advantage in transfer of quantum states
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 12 pages of Supplementary Materials
summary: Quantum advantage, broadly understood as the ability of quantum systems to significantly outperform their classical counterparts, underpins current interest to quantum technologies and is a topic of active investigation. In many situations, its existence is subject to debate, and the areas of supremacy of large-scale quantum systems are not well defined. Here, we uncover a novel niche where quantum advantage can be clearly defined and proven. We study a time-optimal transfer of excitations in the lattice involving both nearest-neighbor and longer-range couplings. We prove that the quantum-mechanical property of a particle to propagate along several trajectories simultaneously speeds up the transfer process, which takes a shorter time compared to any particular trajectory and thus provides a clear example of quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: Quantum advantage demonstrated in time-optimal excitation transfer through quantum superposition enabling faster propagation than any classical trajectory.
AI.motivation: Quantum advantage is often debated and poorly defined for large-scale systems; this work aims to identify a clear, provable niche where quantum systems demonstrably outperform classical counterparts.
AI.method: Study time-optimal transfer of excitations in a lattice with both nearest-neighbor and longer-range couplings, analyzing quantum superposition effects on propagation speed.
AI.result: Proved that quantum superposition (particle propagating along multiple trajectories simultaneously) speeds up transfer process, achieving shorter transfer times than any single classical trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Identified a specific, well-defined scenario where quantum advantage is clearly demonstrable and provable, providing a concrete example of quantum systems outperforming classical ones through superposition effects.

title: Distributed Quantum Property Testing with Communication Constraints
summary: We introduce a framework for distributed quantum inference under communication constraints. In our model, $m$ distributed nodes each receive one copy of an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state $ρ$, before communicating via a constrained one-way communication channel with a central node, which aims to infer some property of $ρ$. This framework generalizes the classical distributed inference framework introduced by Acharya, Canonne, and Tyagi [COLT2019], by allowing quantum resources such as quantum communication and shared entanglement. Within this setting, we focus on the fundamental problem of quantum state certification: Given a complete description of some state $σ$, decide whether $ρ=σ$ or $\|ρ-σ\|_1\geq ε$. Additionally, we focus on the case of limited quantum communication between distributed nodes and the central node. We show that when each communication channel is limited to only $n_q\leq \log d$ qubits, then the sample complexity of distributed state certification is $\mathcal{O}(\frac{d^2}{2^{n_q}ε^2})$ when public randomness is available to all nodes. Moreover, under the assumption that the channels used by the distributed nodes are mixedness-preserving, we prove a matching lower bound. We further demonstrate that shared randomness is necessary to achieve the above complexity, by proving an $Ω(\frac{d^3}{4^{n_q} ε^2})$ lower bound in the private-coin setting under the same assumption as above. Our lower bounds leverage a recently introduced quantum analogue of the celebrated Ingster-Suslina method and generalize arguments from the classical setting. Together, our work provides the first characterization of distributed quantum state certification in the regime of limited quantum communication and establishes a general framework for distributed quantum inference with communication constraints.

AI.tldr: Distributed quantum state certification framework with communication constraints, showing optimal sample complexity of O(d²/(2^{n_q}ε²)) with public randomness and proving matching lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Extend classical distributed inference to quantum setting with communication constraints, focusing on fundamental problem of quantum state certification where distributed nodes receive copies of unknown state and communicate limited quantum information to central node.
AI.method: Generalize classical distributed inference framework to quantum resources (quantum communication, shared entanglement), analyze quantum state certification problem with limited quantum communication (n_q ≤ log d qubits per channel), use quantum analogue of Ingster-Suslina method for lower bounds, consider both public and private randomness settings.
AI.result: With public randomness: sample complexity O(d²/(2^{n_q}ε²)) and matching lower bound under mixedness-preserving channel assumption. With private randomness: Ω(d³/(4^{n_q}ε²)) lower bound, showing shared randomness is necessary for optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: First characterization of distributed quantum state certification under limited quantum communication, establishing general framework for distributed quantum inference with communication constraints and demonstrating importance of shared randomness.

title: Distributions of Noisy Expectation Values over Sets of Measurement Operators
summary: Expectation values of measurement operators, interpreted as measurement probabilities, arise frequently throughout quantum algorithms. When quantum states are randomly distributed, their expectation values are also randomly distributed. In this work, with the goal of understanding non-unitary dynamics, we generalize previous derivations for distributions of expectation values (Campos Venuti and Zanardi, Physics Letters A (377), 2013) to the case of sets of measurement operators and random mixed quantum states within variable sized environments. Using combinatorics approaches, we derive expressions for their moments. We proceed to construct empirical distributions of simulated Haar random brickwork quantum circuits with local depolarizing noise, and compare their form to a proposed effective global-depolarizing-like model with variable effective noise scales and environment dimensions. The fitted effective distributions reproduce peak behaviour across circuit depths, noise scales, and system sizes, while deviations in the distribution tails arise from local noise effects. The fit effective model parameters are also shown to vary smoothly and consistently with circuit depth and noise scale. Finally, sets of non-symmetric measurement operators are shown to exhibit distinct multi-modal distributions relative to uni-modal distributions for symmetric measurement operators, opening up questions about their simulability.

AI.tldr: Distribution analysis of expectation values for measurement operators under random quantum states and non-unitary dynamics, comparing simulated noisy circuits to effective global-depolarizing models.
AI.motivation: To understand non-unitary dynamics in quantum systems by analyzing distributions of expectation values for measurement operators under random quantum states, extending previous work to mixed states and variable environments.
AI.method: Generalize previous derivations using combinatorics to obtain moment expressions for expectation value distributions; construct empirical distributions from simulated Haar random brickwork circuits with local depolarizing noise; compare to proposed effective global-depolarizing-like model with variable parameters.
AI.result: Effective distributions reproduce peak behavior across circuit depths, noise scales, and system sizes; fitted parameters vary smoothly with circuit depth and noise scale; non-symmetric measurement operators exhibit multi-modal distributions versus uni-modal for symmetric operators.
AI.conclusion: The effective global-depolarizing model captures main features of expectation value distributions in noisy quantum circuits, with deviations in tails revealing local noise effects; distinct distribution patterns for symmetric vs. non-symmetric operators raise questions about simulability.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for particle scattering entanglement classification
summary: Entanglement is a key quantity for characterizing quantum correlations in particle scattering processes, but its direct evaluation is computationally demanding on quantum hardware. In this work, we investigate whether fermion density profiles, which are easier to access, can serve as proxies for entanglement by framing the problem as a classification task across multiple entanglement thresholds. Using the fermion scattering in the Thirring model as a test bed, we compare Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNNs) with classical CNNs of comparable parameter counts, and find that QCNNs achieve consistently competitive or superior accuracy with faster convergence and lower variance. Notably, we observe that increasing the model size does not improve the performance within the architectures studied here, and larger models appear to be more sensitive to the choice of encoding. Instead, a compact 4-qubits QCNN provides the best results, suggesting the importance of trainability and encoding choices over model scaling. These findings demonstrate the potential of quantum and quantum-inspired machine learning models for extracting nontrivial quantum information from accessible observables, with implications for high-energy physics and quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: QCNNs outperform classical CNNs in classifying entanglement thresholds from fermion density profiles in the Thirring model, with compact 4-qubit models showing best performance due to trainability and encoding advantages.
AI.motivation: Direct evaluation of entanglement in particle scattering processes is computationally demanding on quantum hardware, motivating the search for easier-to-access proxies like fermion density profiles.
AI.method: Framed as classification across multiple entanglement thresholds using fermion scattering in the Thirring model as test bed; compared Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNNs) with classical CNNs of comparable parameter counts.
AI.result: QCNNs achieve consistently competitive or superior accuracy with faster convergence and lower variance than classical CNNs; increasing model size doesn't improve performance; compact 4-qubit QCNN provides best results.
AI.conclusion: Quantum and quantum-inspired ML models show potential for extracting nontrivial quantum information from accessible observables, with implications for high-energy physics and quantum many-body systems; trainability and encoding choices are more important than model scaling.

title: Scaling Laws for Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks: Depth, Width, and Quantum-Centric Diagnostics
summary: Hybrid quantum neural networks are increasingly explored for classification, yet it remains unclear how their performance and quantum behavior scale with circuit depth and qubit count. We present a controlled scaling study of hybrid quantum-classical classifiers along two axes: (1) increasing the number of quantum layers L at fixed qubits Q, and (2) increasing the number of qubits Q at fixed depth L. Across multiple datasets, we evaluate predictive performance using Accuracy, PR-AUC, Precision, Recall, and F1, and track quantum-specific metrics (QCE, EEE, QGN) to characterize how quantum properties evolve under scaling. Our results summarize scaling trends, saturation regimes, and dataset-dependent sensitivity, and further analyze how quantum metrics relate to predictive performance. This study provides practical guidance for selecting (Q,L) in hybrid QNN classifiers and establishes a consistent evaluation protocol for scaling analysis.

AI.tldr: Scaling study of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks analyzing performance and quantum behavior across circuit depth and qubit count dimensions.
AI.motivation: There is limited understanding of how hybrid quantum neural network performance and quantum behavior scale with circuit depth and qubit count, creating a need for systematic scaling analysis to guide practical implementation.
AI.method: Controlled scaling study along two axes: (1) increasing quantum layers L at fixed qubits Q, and (2) increasing qubits Q at fixed depth L. Evaluation across multiple datasets using predictive metrics (Accuracy, PR-AUC, Precision, Recall, F1) and quantum-specific metrics (QCE, EEE, QGN) to track quantum property evolution.
AI.result: Identified scaling trends, saturation regimes, and dataset-dependent sensitivity. Analyzed relationships between quantum metrics and predictive performance, providing insights into how quantum properties evolve under scaling.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidance for selecting (Q,L) parameters in hybrid QNN classifiers and establishes a consistent evaluation protocol for scaling analysis in quantum machine learning.

title: Exploring bosonic bound states with parallel reaction coordinates
summary: Bound states are dissipation-resilient states that may emerge when quantum systems are strongly coupled to reservoirs with band gaps. We analyze an exactly solvable bosonic model for bound state existence and reproduce these results by a weak-coupling treatment of a supersystem composed of the original system and multiple reaction coordinates, which are individually representing small energy intervals of the reservoir spectral function. Within the perturbative supersystem treatment, the bound state stability results from its energy being inside the band gap. We discuss cases of multiple band gaps and also show that already in presence of weak interactions the bound state's lifetime is finite -- but can be increased by raising the system-reservoir coupling strength.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes bound states in quantum systems strongly coupled to reservoirs with band gaps, showing these states are dissipation-resilient and can be understood through a supersystem approach with multiple reaction coordinates.
AI.motivation: To understand the existence and stability of bound states in quantum systems strongly coupled to reservoirs with band gaps, and to develop analytical approaches for studying these dissipation-resilient states.
AI.method: Uses an exactly solvable bosonic model to analyze bound state existence, and develops a weak-coupling treatment of a supersystem composed of the original system plus multiple reaction coordinates representing small energy intervals of the reservoir spectral function.
AI.result: Bound state stability results from its energy being inside the band gap; the approach works for multiple band gaps; weak interactions make bound state lifetime finite but can be increased by raising system-reservoir coupling strength.
AI.conclusion: Bound states in quantum systems coupled to band-gapped reservoirs are dissipation-resilient, can be analyzed through supersystem approaches, and their lifetime can be controlled by coupling strength even in the presence of weak interactions.

title: Simulating Thermal Properties of Bose-Hubbard Models on a Quantum Computer
summary: While recent advances have established efficient quantum algorithms for preparing Gibbs states of finite-dimensional systems, comparable complexity results for bosonic and other infinite-dimensional models remain unexplored. We introduce the first general rigorous Gibbs sampling framework for bosonic many-body systems, showing that physically relevant bosonic models admit gapped dissipative generators, enabling efficient preparation of thermal states. Although our results hold for broad classes of models, we illustrate them using Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians, both within and beyond the mean-field regime. In both cases, we show that the associated dissipative generators maintain a positive spectral gap, thereby implying exponential convergence to the thermal state. Our argument in the multi-mode case is based on a finite-rank reduction of the dissipative dynamics, which allows us to control the generator via compact perturbations and deduce the discreteness of the spectrum and the stability of the gap. We apply our results to provide efficient preparation of the corresponding Gibbs state on qubit hardware, and by that a quantum algorithm to compute thermal properties of the associated model. This provides the first mathematically controlled route to Gibbs sampling in infinite-dimensional systems, with implications for quantum simulation, thermalization, and many-body complexity, where quantum advantages may arise.

AI.tldr: First rigorous framework for efficient Gibbs state preparation in bosonic many-body systems using gapped dissipative generators, with applications to Bose-Hubbard models and quantum algorithms.
AI.motivation: While efficient quantum algorithms exist for preparing Gibbs states of finite-dimensional systems, comparable complexity results for bosonic and infinite-dimensional models remain unexplored, creating a gap in understanding thermal state preparation for physically relevant bosonic systems.
AI.method: Introduces a general Gibbs sampling framework for bosonic many-body systems, showing physically relevant models admit gapped dissipative generators. Uses finite-rank reduction of dissipative dynamics to control generators via compact perturbations, deducing discreteness of spectrum and gap stability. Demonstrates approach with Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians in both mean-field and beyond-mean-field regimes.
AI.result: Shows that dissipative generators for bosonic models maintain positive spectral gap, implying exponential convergence to thermal states. Provides first mathematically controlled route to Gibbs sampling in infinite-dimensional systems. Enables efficient preparation of Gibbs states on qubit hardware and quantum algorithms for computing thermal properties.
AI.conclusion: Establishes first rigorous framework for efficient Gibbs state preparation in bosonic systems, with implications for quantum simulation, thermalization, and many-body complexity where quantum advantages may arise.

title: Gauss law codes and vacuum codes from lattice gauge theories
comment: 82 pages + appendices, 6 figures. See also the related simultaneous submission by Rothlin et al. Comments welcome
summary: We develop a comprehensive framework for constructing quantum error correcting codes (QECCs) from Abelian lattice gauge theories (LGTs) using quantum reference frames (QRFs) as a unifying formalism. We consider LGTs with arbitrary compact Abelian gauge groups supported on lattices in arbitrary numbers of spatial dimensions, and we work with both pure gauge theories and theories with couplings to bosonic and fermionic matter. The codes that we construct fall into two classes: First, Gauss law codes identify the code subspace with the full gauge-invariant sector of the theory. In models with matter coupled to gauge fields, these codes inherit a natural subsystem structure in which gauge-invariant Wilson loops and dressed matter excitations factorize the code space. Second, vacuum codes restrict the code subspace to the matter vacuum sector within the gauge-invariant subspace, yielding codes where errors correspond to gauge-invariant charge excitations rather than to violations of the Gauss law. Despite their distinct setup, we show that when the gauge group is finite, vacuum codes are unitarily equivalent to pure gauge theory Gauss law codes, and that when the group is continuous, this is only true upon a charge coarse-graining of the vacuum code. In all cases, QRFs provide a systematic apparatus for fully characterizing the codes' algebraic structures and correctable error sets. For clarity, we illustrate our general results in $\mathbb{Z}_2$-gauge theory, as well as in scalar and fermionic QED. These findings offer fundamental insights into the parallelism between quantum error correction and gauge theory and point toward practical advantages for simulating LGTs on noisy quantum devices.

AI.tldr: A framework for constructing quantum error correcting codes from Abelian lattice gauge theories using quantum reference frames, yielding two code classes: Gauss law codes and vacuum codes, with applications to quantum simulation.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic connection between quantum error correction and gauge theory, leveraging the parallelism between these fields to construct practical codes for simulating lattice gauge theories on noisy quantum devices.
AI.method: Use quantum reference frames as unifying formalism to construct QECCs from Abelian lattice gauge theories with arbitrary compact gauge groups in any spatial dimensions, considering both pure gauge theories and those coupled to bosonic/fermionic matter.
AI.result: Two code classes emerge: Gauss law codes (full gauge-invariant sector) with natural subsystem structure, and vacuum codes (matter vacuum sector). For finite gauge groups, vacuum codes are unitarily equivalent to pure gauge theory Gauss law codes; for continuous groups, equivalence requires charge coarse-graining.
AI.conclusion: Quantum reference frames provide systematic characterization of code algebraic structures and correctable error sets, offering fundamental insights into gauge theory-QEC parallelism and practical advantages for simulating lattice gauge theories on noisy quantum hardware.

title: Pixel-Translation-Equivariant Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks via Fourier Multiplexers
summary: Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success to hard-coding translation equivariance. Quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) have been proposed as near-term quantum analogues, but the relevant notion of translation depends on the data encoding. For address/amplitude encodings such as FRQI, a pixel shift acts as modular addition on an index register, whereas many MERA-inspired QCNNs are equivariant only under cyclic permutations of physical qubits. We formalize this mismatch and construct QCNN layers that commute exactly with the pixel cyclic shift (PCS) symmetry induced by the encoding. Our main technical result is a constructive characterization of all PCS-equivariant unitaries: conjugation by the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) diagonalizes translations, so any PCS-equivariant layer is a Fourier-mode multiplexer followed by an inverse QFT (IQFT). Building on this characterization, we introduce a deep PCS-QCNN with measurement-induced pooling, deferred conditioning, and inter-layer QFT cancellation. We also analyze trainability at random initialization and prove a lower bound on the expected squared gradient norm that remains constant in a depth-scaling regime, ruling out a depth-induced barren plateau in that sense.

AI.tldr: QCNNs need translation equivariance matching data encoding; paper constructs QCNN layers commuting exactly with pixel cyclic shift symmetry, characterizes all such equivariant unitaries via QFT diagonalization, and introduces deep PCS-QCNN with improved trainability.
AI.motivation: Quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) require translation equivariance, but existing approaches mismatch with data encoding symmetries. Address/amplitude encodings like FRQI induce pixel cyclic shift (PCS) symmetry, while many MERA-inspired QCNNs only handle cyclic permutations of physical qubits. This formal mismatch needs resolution for proper equivariant QCNNs.
AI.method: Characterize all PCS-equivariant unitaries by showing conjugation by quantum Fourier transform (QFT) diagonalizes translations, making any PCS-equivariant layer a Fourier-mode multiplexer followed by inverse QFT. Build deep PCS-QCNN with measurement-induced pooling, deferred conditioning, and inter-layer QFT cancellation.
AI.result: Constructive characterization of all PCS-equivariant unitaries enables exact commutation with pixel cyclic shift symmetry. Deep PCS-QCNN architecture with improved components. Trainability analysis shows constant expected squared gradient norm in depth-scaling regime, ruling out depth-induced barren plateaus.
AI.conclusion: Formalized encoding-dependent translation equivariance in QCNNs, provided complete characterization of PCS-equivariant unitaries via QFT diagonalization, and constructed practical deep PCS-QCNN with proven trainability guarantees, addressing fundamental symmetry mismatch in quantum convolutional architectures.

title: Nonvariational quantum optimisation approaches to pangenome-guided sequence assembly
summary: Assembling genomes from short-read sequencing data remains difficult in repetitive regions, where reference bias and combinatorial complexity limit existing methods. Pangenome-guided sequence assembly (PGSA) mitigates reference bias by reconstructing an individual genome as a walk through a population-level graph. The associated problem, identifying a walk whose node visits match read-derived copy numbers, is NP-hard and already challenges classical solvers at a moderate scale. We develop near-term quantum optimisation approaches for this computational bottleneck. We consider two problem encodings: an established quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation and a new higher-order binary optimisation (HUBO) formulation. The latter reduces the number of variables from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N\log N)$ and places moderate-sized instances within the qubit budget of current devices. We solve both using the Iterative-QAOA framework, which combines a fixed linear-ramp QAOA schedule with iterative warm-start bias updates, avoiding the overhead of full variational parameter optimisation. A custom circuit compilation strategy reduces hardware gate overhead by up to 67\% compared with standard tools. In noiseless simulations of QUBO problems, Iterative-QAOA reliably identifies optimal assemblies from as few as $10^{-17}\%$ of all candidate solutions, and \textit{IBM} quantum hardware closely reproduces relevant results with sufficient sampling via CVaR-style post-selection. For HUBO, the variable reduction comes at the cost of deeper compiled circuits and greater noise sensitivity: an expected qubit--depth trade-off. Our findings establish pangenome assembly as a concrete, biologically motivated problem class at the scale where quantum optimisation may first provide practical value.

AI.tldr: Quantum optimization approaches (Iterative-QAOA) for pangenome-guided sequence assembly, addressing NP-hard combinatorial problems with QUBO and HUBO formulations to overcome reference bias in repetitive genomic regions.
AI.motivation: Assembling genomes from short-read data is challenging in repetitive regions due to reference bias and combinatorial complexity. Existing methods struggle with NP-hard problems at moderate scales, creating a computational bottleneck that quantum optimization could potentially address.
AI.method: Developed near-term quantum optimization using Iterative-QAOA framework with two problem encodings: QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimization) and new HUBO (higher-order binary optimization) formulation. HUBO reduces variables from O(N²) to O(N log N). Custom circuit compilation reduces hardware gate overhead by up to 67%. Uses fixed linear-ramp QAOA schedule with iterative warm-start bias updates, avoiding full variational parameter optimization.
AI.result: In noiseless simulations, Iterative-QAOA reliably identifies optimal assemblies from as few as 10⁻¹⁷% of all candidate solutions. IBM quantum hardware closely reproduces relevant results with sufficient sampling via CVaR-style post-selection. HUBO formulation achieves variable reduction but at cost of deeper compiled circuits and greater noise sensitivity (qubit-depth trade-off).
AI.conclusion: Pangenome assembly represents a concrete, biologically motivated problem class at the scale where quantum optimization may first provide practical value, establishing a promising application domain for near-term quantum devices.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for the N-representability of functionals of the one-electron reduced density matrix
summary: We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the N-representability of the universal one-electron reduced density matrix functional. Functionals satisfying these conditions are guaranteed to yield variational upper bounds on the true energy in one-electron reduced density matrix functional theory, regardless of the strength of the interparticle repulsion. Conversely, any functional violating these conditions will necessarily underestimate the true energy for certain systems. These exact constraints impose a stringent restriction on density matrix functional approximations, as many existing functionals-including the Hartree-Fock functional-appear to violate them. This mathematical formalism, therefore, can guide the development of new approximate functionals and numerical algorithms.
