AI.tldr: Establishes exact N-representability conditions for 1-RDM functionals that guarantee variational upper bounds on true energy, regardless of interaction strength, with implications for functional development.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous mathematical constraints for one-electron reduced density matrix (1-RDM) functional theory that ensure variational upper bounds on the true energy, addressing limitations of existing approximations that may violate these conditions.
AI.method: Develops necessary and sufficient conditions for N-representability of universal 1-RDM functionals using mathematical formalism to establish exact constraints that guarantee variational upper bounds.
AI.result: Establishes exact constraints that many existing functionals (including Hartree-Fock) violate, showing these violations lead to energy underestimation for certain systems, while functionals satisfying conditions guarantee variational upper bounds regardless of interaction strength.
AI.conclusion: The derived N-representability conditions provide stringent restrictions for density matrix functional approximations and can guide development of new functionals and numerical algorithms with guaranteed variational properties.

title: Shot-Based Quantum Encoding: A Data-Loading Paradigm for Quantum Neural Networks
summary: Efficient data loading remains a bottleneck for near-term quantum machine-learning. Existing schemes (angle, amplitude, and basis encoding) either underuse the exponential Hilbert-space capacity or require circuit depths that exceed the coherence budgets of noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. We introduce Shot-Based Quantum Encoding (SBQE), a data embedding strategy that distributes the hardware's native resource, shots, according to a data-dependent classical distribution over multiple initial quantum states. By treating the shot counts as a learnable degree of freedom, SBQE produces a mixed-state representation whose expectation values are linear in the classical probabilities and can therefore be composed with non-linear activation functions. We show that SBQE is structurally equivalent to a multilayer perceptron whose weights are realised by quantum circuits, and we describe a hardware-compatible implementation protocol. Benchmarks on Fashion MNIST and Semeion handwritten digits, with ten independent initialisations per model, show that SBQE achieves 89.1% +/- 0.9% test accuracy on Semeion (reducing error by 5.3% relative to amplitude encoding and matching a width-matched classical network) and 80.95% +/- 0.10% on Fashion MNIST (exceeding amplitude encoding by +2.0% and a linear multilayer perceptron by +1.3%), all without any data-encoding gates.

AI.tldr: SBQE is a novel quantum encoding method that uses shot distribution over multiple initial states as a learnable resource, enabling linear expectation values compatible with non-linear activations without data-encoding gates.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum encoding schemes (angle, amplitude, basis encoding) either underutilize Hilbert-space capacity or require circuit depths exceeding coherence budgets of NISQ hardware, creating a bottleneck for quantum machine learning data loading.
AI.method: Shot-Based Quantum Encoding (SBQE) distributes hardware's native resource (shots) according to a data-dependent classical distribution over multiple initial quantum states, treating shot counts as learnable degrees of freedom to produce mixed-state representations with linear expectation values.
AI.result: SBQE achieves 89.1% ± 0.9% test accuracy on Semeion (5.3% error reduction vs amplitude encoding, matching width-matched classical network) and 80.95% ± 0.10% on Fashion MNIST (+2.0% vs amplitude encoding, +1.3% vs linear multilayer perceptron).
AI.conclusion: SBQE provides an efficient data encoding strategy for NISQ hardware that avoids data-encoding gates, enables compatibility with non-linear activations, and demonstrates competitive performance on benchmark datasets while utilizing hardware's native shot resource as a learnable parameter.

title: Light-Induced Quantum Self-Trapping of Vibrational Excitons in an Optical Cavity
summary: In an optical cavity, strong light--matter coupling between excitons and photons has been widely reported as a way to enhance energy delocalization through spatially extended polaritonic states. In contrast, leveraging cavity-mediated light--matter effects to promote the reciprocal phenomenon, namely \textit{energy localization}, remains largely underexplored. In the present work, we address this question by focusing on a special form of energy localization arising from nonlinear matter interactions: \textit{Quantum Self-Trapping} (QST). We employ a generalized Tavis--Cummings model to investigate the transport of vibrational excitons -- \textit{i.e., vibrons} -- between two anharmonic vibrational modes and examine their interplay with cavity photons. In the absence of a cavity, the arising of true and complete QST -- \textit{i.e.}, an infinite-lifetime localization -- is not possible due to the symmetry of the system. The energy transfer between the two modes still occurs, slowed down by the many-body interactions. Coupling the system to a single-mode cavity strongly alters this behavior, with two emerging regimes. First, at weak light--matter coupling, destructive interference between newly opened transition pathways suppresses energy exchange, leading to cavity-enhanced self-trapping. As the coupling strength increases, these interference effects evolve leading to cavity-assisted energy transfer, where we observe an acceleration of the vibrational energy flow. Most notably, we identify critical coupling strengths that separate both regimes in which the dynamics almost totally freeze, suggesting the arising of a ``stabilized'' light-induced~QST of many-vibron bound states. These results suggest that optical cavities can not only enhance transport but could also stabilize energy localization phenomena, providing a new route to control energy flow in quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Cavity quantum electrodynamics enables control of vibrational energy localization (quantum self-trapping) and transfer between anharmonic modes via interference effects, with regimes of cavity-enhanced self-trapping and cavity-assisted energy transfer separated by critical coupling strengths.
AI.motivation: While optical cavities are known to enhance energy delocalization through polaritonic states, their potential to promote energy localization phenomena like quantum self-trapping remains largely unexplored. The paper aims to investigate how cavity-mediated light-matter interactions can control and stabilize energy localization in quantum systems.
AI.method: A generalized Tavis-Cummings model is employed to study transport of vibrational excitons (vibrons) between two anharmonic vibrational modes coupled to cavity photons. The approach examines the interplay between nonlinear matter interactions and cavity quantum electrodynamics effects.
AI.result: Without cavity coupling, complete quantum self-trapping is impossible due to system symmetry, though many-body interactions slow energy transfer. Cavity coupling creates two regimes: weak coupling leads to destructive interference suppressing energy exchange (cavity-enhanced self-trapping), while strong coupling enables cavity-assisted accelerated energy transfer. Critical coupling strengths separate regimes where dynamics nearly freeze, suggesting stabilized light-induced quantum self-trapping of many-vibron bound states.
AI.conclusion: Optical cavities can not only enhance energy transport but also stabilize energy localization phenomena like quantum self-trapping, providing a new mechanism to control quantum energy flow through interference effects and critical coupling strengths.

title: From generating functions to the geometric Binder cumulant
summary: We present an overview of the role of generating functions in quantum mechanical contexts, mainly in the modern theory of polarization and in the study of quantum phase transitions. Generating functions enable the derivation of moments and cumulants, quantities which characterize the fluctuations of an underlying probability distribution. In all of the cases we review, the fluctuations are those of a quantum system. We show that the original formalism for geometric phases, in which a quantum system is taken around an adiabatic cycle, can be extended to the case when degeneracy points are encountered along the cycle (quasiadiabatic cycles). The essential tool for this extension is a generalized Bargmann invariant which plays the role of a generating function. From the cumulants generated this way one can form ratios according to the Binder cumulant scheme in statistical mechanics. Such geometric Binder cumulants are sensitive to gap closure, as such, they are useful in identifying metal-insulator transitions, localization, and quantum phase transitions. We present example calculations on simple model systems, whose localization properties are well known, to validate to approach. We also complement our geometric Binder cumulant calculations with results for the fidelity susceptibility, a quantity directly related to the quantum geometry of the parameter space.

AI.tldr: Generating functions in quantum mechanics enable derivation of moments/cumulants characterizing quantum fluctuations; extended geometric phase formalism to quasiadiabatic cycles using generalized Bargmann invariants; geometric Binder cumulants detect gap closure for identifying quantum phase transitions, validated on model systems.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the utility of generating functions in quantum mechanical contexts, particularly for extending geometric phase formalism to quasiadiabatic cycles and developing sensitive indicators for quantum phase transitions based on fluctuations and cumulants.
AI.method: Extend original geometric phase formalism using generalized Bargmann invariants as generating functions; derive cumulants from these generating functions; form geometric Binder cumulants following statistical mechanics scheme; validate approach on simple model systems with known localization properties; complement with fidelity susceptibility calculations.
AI.result: Geometric Binder cumulants derived from generating functions are sensitive to gap closure and useful for identifying metal-insulator transitions, localization, and quantum phase transitions; approach validated on model systems; fidelity susceptibility provides complementary quantum geometric information.
AI.conclusion: Generating functions provide powerful framework for analyzing quantum fluctuations and extending geometric phase concepts; geometric Binder cumulants offer sensitive probes for quantum phase transitions; combined approach with fidelity susceptibility provides comprehensive characterization of quantum systems' geometric properties.

title: Error Correction in Lattice Quantum Electrodynamics with Quantum Reference Frames
comment: 41+22 pages, 8 figures. See also the related simultaneous submission by Lacambra et al
summary: Is gauge symmetry merely a redundancy in our description, or does it carry a deeper information-theoretic significance? Quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) show that redundancy can serve as a resource for protecting information against noise. In this work, we ask whether gauge theories can be understood in similar terms, and make this idea concrete in lattice quantum electrodynamics (QED), building on and extending earlier works that established a bridge between gauge systems, stabilizer codes, and quantum reference frames (QRFs). For Abelian gauge groups, we show that explicit recovery operations can be constructed using group-theoretical methods for error sets determined by both ideal and non-ideal QRFs. Applied to lattice QED, this yields two QECC structures: one in the pure-gauge sector and one including fermions. We construct a gauge-field QRF based on spanning trees of the lattice and a fermionic field QRF from the matter field, thereby making explicit how physical information is encoded. While the syndromes of gauge-violating errors associated with constraint measurements are generically degenerate, QRFs resolve this degeneracy and single out families of correctable errors. This establishes lattice QED as a QECC beyond the stabilizer setting and shows concretely how gauge symmetry provides an encoding structure that supports error correction.

AI.tldr: Lattice QED can be understood as a quantum error-correcting code where gauge symmetry provides an encoding structure, with explicit recovery operations constructed using group theory and quantum reference frames.
AI.motivation: To determine whether gauge symmetry has deeper information-theoretic significance beyond being merely a redundancy in description, by exploring connections between gauge theories, quantum error correction, and quantum reference frames.
AI.method: Construct explicit recovery operations using group-theoretical methods for Abelian gauge groups, applied to lattice QED. Build gauge-field quantum reference frames based on spanning trees and fermionic field QRFs from matter fields. Use these QRFs to resolve degeneracy in gauge-violating error syndromes.

AI.conclusion: Gauge symmetry provides an encoding structure that supports error correction, demonstrating that gauge theories can be understood as quantum error-correcting codes with explicit recovery operations constructed via group theory and quantum reference frames.
